articles.title: Is it the end of the road for Tesla's Cybertruck?
articles.summary: The car company's CEO Elon Musk has said production will halt in Texas, to focus on the firm's self-driving Cybercabs.
articles.body:
Tesla CEO Elon Musk has said production of the firm's Cybertruck is "winding down" in Texas, to focus on its self-driving Cybercab cars.

The model is only produced at Tesla's Austin base, and he did not clarify if manufacturing would be moved elsewhere or simply cease.

The Cybertruck has received a mixed response since its launch in 2023, with some praising its individuality and others simply labelling it ugly.

It has also suffered from disappointing sales, quality problems and recalls.

articles.title: What is climate change? A really simple guide
articles.summary: Human activities are causing the world to heat up, posing serious threats to people and nature.
articles.body:
Human activities are causing world temperatures to rise, posing serious threats to people and nature.

Things are likely to worsen in the coming decades, but scientists argue urgent action can still limit the worst effects of climate change.

Climate change is the long-term shift in the Earth's average temperatures and weather conditions.

The world has been rapidly warming for around a century, causing weather patterns to change.

Since the 1980s, each decade has been warmer than the previous one, the Met Office says.

2024 was Earth's hottest year on record , with climate change mainly responsible for the high temperatures.

It was also the first calendar year to surpass 1.5C of warming compared to "pre-industrial" levels of the late 1800s, according to the Copernicus climate service .

Temperatures remained high in 2025 , despite a slight cooling from a natural weather pattern called La Niña.

The opposite El Niño pattern , combined with climate change, makes it likely that 2026 will also rank among the hottest years ever recorded.

The climate has changed naturally throughout the Earth's history.

But natural causes cannot explain the particularly rapid warming seen over the last century, according to the UN's climate body, the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change (IPCC).

This has been without doubt caused by human activities, especially the widespread use of fossil fuels - coal, oil and gas - in homes, factories and transport systems.

When fossil fuels burn, they release greenhouse gases - mostly carbon dioxide (CO2). This CO2 acts like a blanket, trapping extra energy in the atmosphere near the Earth's surface. This causes the planet to heat up.

Since the start of the Industrial Revolution - when humans began burning large amounts of fossil fuels - the level of CO2 in the atmosphere has risen by more than 50% .

The CO2 released from burning fossil fuels has a distinctive chemical fingerprint. This matches the type of CO2 increasingly found in the atmosphere.

What effects of climate change have already been seen?

Climate change has already had a huge effect, including:

more frequent and intense extreme weather , such as heatwaves and heavy rainfall

rapid melting of glaciers and ice sheets, contributing to sea-level rises

warmer oceans , which can fuel more intense storms and harm sea life

These changes are already having serious consequences for people and economies around the world.

Flash floods in Nepal killed more than 1,400 people in August 2026. Nepal's Finance Minister, Swarnim Wagle, said it could cost up to a tenth of the economy to rebuild.

Climate change increased the chances of the glacier collapse which triggered the flood, World Weather Attribution group scientists said.

Why does 1.5C matter and how will future climate change affect the world?

The more the world warms, the worse the impacts of climate change become.

Nearly 200 countries pledged to try to limit global warming to 1.5C above pre-industrial levels in the 2015 Paris agreement .

That target is generally understood to mean an average annual increase of 1.5C over 20 years rather than a one-off rise in a single year.

Long-term warming of 1.5C would bring serious consequences for many populations.

But an increase of 2C or more would bring even greater impacts, the IPCC says.

increased risks to food security in some regions due to more extreme weather

greater chances of some climate-sensitive diseases spreading, such as dengue

more species being threatened with extinction

The call to restrict temperature rise to 1.5C was partly designed to avoid crossing so-called "tipping points".

It is not clear exactly where they sit, but once these thresholds are passed, changes could accelerate and become irreversible.

These could include the collapse of the Greenland Ice Sheet , warm Atlantic Ocean currents or further loss of the Amazon rainforest .

About 3.3 to 3.6 billion people are highly vulnerable to climate change, the IPCC says.

People living in poorer countries are expected to suffer most as they have fewer resources to adapt.

This has led to questions about fairness , because these places have typically only been responsible for a small percentage of greenhouse gas emissions.

However, knock-on impacts could be felt over wide areas. For example, crop failures linked to extreme weather could raise food prices globally.

What are governments doing about climate change?

Reaching net zero CO2 emissions is essential to limit global warming, the IPCC says.

This means reducing emissions as much as possible and actively removing any remaining emissions from the atmosphere.

There has been encouraging progress in some areas, such as renewable energy and electric vehicles.

But humanity's CO2 emissions are still at record highs , causing long-term warming to reach 1.4C in 2025.

The latest UN Emissions Gap Report said the 1.5C limit was likely to be breached in the coming years.

A return to 1.5C by 2100 was possible, but it would require "urgent and stringent cuts to greenhouse emissions", the report added.

Otherwise, global warming could reach nearly 3C by the end of the century, the UN said.

World leaders meet every year to discuss their climate commitments.

In 2025, the COP30 climate conference ended without any new agreements on fossil fuels or deforestation in the final deal.

Countries had previously agreed on the need to "transition away from fossil fuels in energy systems" at the COP28 talks in 2023.

At COP29 in 2024, richer countries committed to giving developing nations at least $300bn (£223bn) a year by 2035 to help them tackle climate change. But this is far less than poorer countries say they need.

What can individuals do about climate change?

Major changes need to come from governments and businesses, but individuals can help through actions like:

improving their home's insulation and energy efficiency

switching to electric vehicles or living car-free

replacing gas boilers with electric systems like heat pumps

articles.title: Smugglers are reportedly soldering top-tier HBM onto deliberately useless processors to sneak it into China, and the trick isn't new
articles.summary: Smugglers are reportedly gluing $4,000 HBM stacks to processors nobody would buy, then taking them apart in Shenzhen.
articles.body:

Smugglers are reportedly pairing Samsung and SK hynix HBM with deliberately useless processors so the package passes export regulations as a low-end chip

Shenzhen workshops then heat the packages, pry off the HBM3E, and sell it for about $4,000 a stack, mostly to Huawei customers

The trick exploits a December 2024 BIS exclusion for co-packaged chips, but only "where the dominant function" is processing

Some of the most sought-after memory in the AI industry is reportedly reaching China attached to processors that were designed never to be used.

A new report from The Information claims smugglers are taking high-bandwidth memory (HBM) made by Samsung and SK hynix, packaging it alongside cheap, low-performance server chips, and exporting the combination as an ordinary processor with a CPU that nobody really wants.

Once the packages reach mainland China, workshops heat them until the solder gives way, pry off the memory stacks, and discard the processors.

A processor nobody wants paired to memory that has Chinese buyers lining up for more

The scheme reached a much wider audience when Chinese tech commentator AB Kuai.Dong summarized the report for his followers on X , describing the decoy chips as "clunky" processors and calling the arrangement a "compliant export.

Reporting from Wccftech sheds more light on the smuggler at the center of the story: a man in his 40s, fluent in Chinese and Korean, with a background in the Korean chip industry.

He runs what is on paper an ordinary chip design firm with an interesting caveat: Its processors are reportedly so weak that no data center would buy them, which is the point: they give the company a reason to order top-tier HBM in volume.

Packaging houses in Taiwan, South Korea and Southeast Asia then reportedly bond the memory and the processor onto a single substrate, and the package ships to Hong Kong declared for export reasons as a processor. From there, it crosses into the mainland in luggage, car trunks, and the bags of daily cross-border commuters, being smuggled en masse to Chinese workshops.

The last step is arguably the riskiest: Seoul Economic Daily reports that excessive or overly rapid heat can warp or crack the memory stacks, and that failure rates are high. The margins are large enough that nobody involved minds the potential risk.

Skirting export compliance at $4,000 a stack

The entire process is possible due to a gap that sits in the rules the US Commerce Department's Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS) published in December 2024 . Those rules require a license to ship standalone HBM with a bandwidth density above 2GB/s/mm^2 to China, but a technical note excludes co-packaged chips that combine HBM and logic.

Those are instead judged by the package's processing performance. Pair a fast memory stack with a slow processor, and you get a chip cleared for export even if the primary goal is to secure the HBM rather than the underlying chip.

To its credit, the BIS did anticipate this in some form: The same note keeps HBM under control when it is permanently affixed to a logic die that merely serves as a control interface to the physical layer, so a memory stack sitting on a thin controller does not escape.

What it did not account for was a processor engineered to be useless. Interestingly, the exclusion applies, in the regulator's own words, only "where the dominant function of the co-packaged integrated circuit is processing." It is hard to argue that processing is the dominant function of a package whose value lies almost entirely in its memory.

Nothing about this approach is new: In April 2025, SemiAnalysis reported that CoAsia Electronics, Samsung's HBM distributor in Greater China, was shipping HBM2E to Taiwanese design services firm Faraday Technology, which had SPIL package it with a low-cost 16nm logic die before sending it on to China, where the memory could reportedly be desoldered. "The HBM export ban is specifically for raw HBM packages," the analysts wrote.

Faraday denied breaching export rules and said it had no ties to Huawei. Company president Steve Wang went further, telling the Taipei Times that "It is impossible to recover an HBM unit through desoldering." A year and a half later, The Information's sources describe Shenzhen workshops doing precisely that even as the approach remains relatively risky.

By September 2025, SemiAnalysis believed the CoAsia and Faraday flow had stopped, though it estimated China had already amassed about 13 million HBM stacks, including 11.4 million directly from Samsung, some 7 million of them in the month between the December 2024 rule's announcement and its subsequent enforcement.

Teardowns have already found Samsung and SK hynix memory inside Huawei's Ascend 910C. As recently as February 2026, AI Frontiers described the packaged HBM breach as apparently contained, while urging BIS to issue red-flag warnings on packaged HBM deployed in ways that tend to "allow the memory to be easily removed from finished chips after export."

If The Information's sources are correct, the technique was never really contained, only made quieter. It has moved up a generation to HBM3E and spread. At $4,000 a stack and willing buyers available across the board, it isn't altogether surprising either.

A Shenzhen broker in his early 20s, about three years into the trade, told The Information that a single HBM3E stack sold for a few hundred dollars in China a year ago. "Today it's about $4,000," he said, highlighting a near-tenfold increase in price due to an HBM-starved Chinese market.

With six to eight stacks required per AI accelerator, memory alone comes to $24,000 to $32,000 per chip, before the processor, server, or power bill is even considered.

TrendForce , also citing the same report, states that Huawei has raised the suggested price of its Ascend 950DT to more than RMB 250,000 (about $37,000), blaming memory costs and tight supply. This means that the black-market HBM for a single accelerator would be considerably more than half of the sticker price, though the 950DT's own stack count is not specified.

SK hynix said in a statement carried by SBS News that it complies with US and South Korean export controls and has not supplied Huawei since US restrictions took effect in 2020. Samsung has not directly commented in any coverage so far, and neither BIS nor the South Korean government has said anything publicly. Seoul Economic Daily notes the precedent Korean suppliers will be watching: TSMC faced a US investigation in 2024 after one of its chips was found in a Huawei product.

This is in the backdrop of US enforcement gathering pace as it goes after some of the allegedly worst offenders: In March, prosecutors charged Super Micro co-founder Yih-Shyan Liaw and two others over an alleged $2.5 billion scheme to route servers built on restricted Nvidia chips to China. On October 1, federal agents arrested Greg Lui, CEO of California-based Earthmade Computer, over more than $300 million of export-controlled servers allegedly shipped via Malaysia and Singapore.

The Information's report, however, leans heavily on anonymous dealers, with no shipment volumes, seizures, company names, or failure-rate figures attached. Despite this, the incentives it describes are real, and the method was documented more than 18 months ago by SemiAnalysis.

Until BIS either counts the memory or holds co-packaged chips to that "dominant function" test, the market for processors nobody wants is likely to stay surprisingly healthy and functional even as Chinese AI memory appetite remains voracious.

articles.title: Archaeologists crack a shipwreck’s 400-year-old combination lock
articles.summary: Welsh locals blamed a witch for sinking the 'Ann Francis' in 1583.
articles.body:
Archaeologists have finally cracked the code to the famed Ann Francis shipwreck 's brass combination treasure lock. However, the 16th century relic didn't open after hours of painstaking trial-and-error. Researchers at Cardiff University and Amgueddfa Cymru, the National Museum of Wales, relied on highly detailed CT scanning equipment to peer inside the mechanical device and learn the code without touching the lock itself.

"It's not every day you get to solve a 400-year-old mystery," David Williams , a Cardiff University biomechanics engineer, said in a statement .

The lock's combination was lost on December 28, 1583, when the merchant ship Ann Francis sailed into a powerful storm during a return voyage from Spain. The exact crew number is unclear, but all of them (around 14 sailors) reportedly drowned after veering off-course and wrecking along the coast of southern Wales. Unfortunately, at least one other death is likely directly tied to the Ann Francis . Archival evidence suggests locals later accused a "detestable woman" named Mother Gabley of being an "execrable witch" and casting the foul weather responsible for the maritime tragedy. While Mother Gabley's fate remains unknown, she would have almost certainly been hanged under the recently passed "Act Against Conjurations, Enchantments and Witchcrafts" if brought to trial.

The Ann Francis remained missing for 415 years, until metal detectorist Peter Hughes rediscovered the wreckage while surveying southern Wales' Margam Beach in 1998. Hughes and archaeologists subsequently spent more than 20 years scouring the area for the ship's remains. By 2017, preservationists had documented over 800 gold and silver coins from Germany, Spain, and Portugal along with artifacts like compasses, ship equipment, and cutlery.

Still, the wreck's most famous remnant is the brass combination lock still in working condition after four centuries buried in sand. It's possible the lock was used to guard those coins, or potentially other valuables that didn't survive exposure to the elements. Regardless, the lock has remained close with no hints to its four-letter combination for hundreds of years.

"Elizabethan combination locks are known in Britain, but this one is in exceptionally good condition and is associated with a dated wreck, making it a unique find and the code a tantalizing mystery to solve," said Alastair Willis , senior numismatics curator at Amgueddfa Cymru.

Tampering with the delicate lock was out of the question, but Willis and his colleagues knew what to do. Using micro-computed tomography (micro-CT) scanning, they looked inside the device and determined the correct code.

"By creating a detailed 3D image of the internal mechanism, I could see how the notches lined up with the letters and identify the exact combination," explained Williams, who called the experience "certainly a first" for his team.

The correct four-letter combo? A-N-C-E. But with one longstanding question finally answered, another one has arisen.

"Of course, now we've solved it, we are left wondering if the code meant something to its owner," added Willis.

articles.title: Canadian professor warns massive new data center would release ‘23 Hiroshima-sized atomic bombs worth of energy’ every day
articles.summary: Building Kevin O’Leary’s giant data center would release the equivalent energy of 23 nukes every day.
articles.body:
When you buy through links on our articles, Future and its syndication partners may earn a commission.

Celebrity investor Kevin O'Leary's Wonder Valley data center plans are under scrutiny

The Sturgeon Lake Cree Nation (SLCN) has filed for a judicial review over the project, which is planned to be the world's largest data center

A physicist hired by the SLCN has declared the data center will release significant heat waste

A physicist acting on behalf of the Sturgeon Lake Cree Nation (SLCN) has claimed that the O'Leary Digital Wonder Valley data center would release "23 atomic bombs of energy" while adding that the declaration is "a first-order estimate intended to convey scale."

The report by Utah State University physicist Robert Davies, working on behalf of the SLCN, whose lawyer, also adds that current regulations for developing land are not suited to projects of the data center's scale.

O'Leary Digital Wonder Valley, plans for which were first unveiled in 2024, was conceived to be the largest on the planet when completed, and has a $70 billion budget for the 64 square kilometer (almost 15815 acres) development. Its planned location is in the SLCN's traditional territory in Alberta, Canada.

The planned scale of the data center, earmarked for a location 130 km southwest of the SLCN's reserve, is the main point of contention, and the basis for Professor Robert Davies, of the Utah State University.

But his claim over the "23 atomic bombs of energy" demands some clarification.

"Now of course, that's not explosions, but that's just trying to get a sense of how much energy we're talking about," said Davies in the assessment. "The effect will almost certainly be large, if not extreme."

He also notes that "every quantitative figure … should be treated as a first-order estimate intended to convey scale, to be confirmed against the developer's own filings."

Davies also highlights that the project could be "the largest single-site heat source on the entire planet."

The assessment, which was prepared for SLCN's case, emphasizes that it is "not a comprehensive environmental review, a formal expert report, or a legal opinion."

While Davies' contribution to the SLCN's judicial review filing relies on further information from O'Leary Digital, it paints a worrying picture, not least into the effects of the heat waste on the surrounding wildlife.

"I can't imagine allowing it to go forward without those full assessments," Davies said, while also criticizing the use of traditional environmental legislation and guidelines for giant data center projects. "When people talk about environmental regulations that these projects have to adhere to, those regulations were not created with anything of this scale in mind."

Naturally, O'Leary Digital has responded to the filing. CEO Paul Palandjian wrote in an email "We also respect the robust and stringent regulatory process we must follow in advancing Wonder Valley… we're having productive dialogue with Indigenous communities through consultation and engagement, and we remain committed to that work."

articles.title: Physicists sank a telescope 1.5 miles under the sea to put Einstein's relativity to the test
articles.summary: A half-built neutrino telescope on the floor of the Mediterranean Sea searched for cracks in one of physics' most basic invariances. It came up empty, but it...
articles.body:
When you buy through links on our articles, Future and its syndication partners may earn a commission.

A particle-detecting telescope sunk more than a mile beneath the sea off the coast of France has tested a core principle of Einstein's relativity and found no cracks.

The detector, called Oscillation Research with Cosmics in the Abyss (ORCA) , detects elusive particles called neutrinos. As a doctoral student, Alba Domi rode onto the Mediterranean aboard one of two boats that helped build the telescope, lowering some of its first detection units to the seafloor about 1.5 miles (2.4 kilometers) below the waves off Toulon, France.

Now, data from those first detection units have been used to test one of the founding rules of Einstein's relativity: the idea that the laws of nature look the same no matter which way you face or how fast you move.

The team found no sign that this rule, called Lorentz invariance, is broken. But even with a detector only a fraction of its planned size, they set limits that compete with those of far larger and longer-running experiments.

The results were published Wednesday (Nov. 4) in the Journal of Cosmology and Astroparticle Physics.

Physics rests on two successful theories: general relativity , conceived by Albert Einstein more than 100 years ago, and the Standard Model of subatomic physics.

"General relativity describes the universe well on a cosmic scale, and the Standard Model of particle physics describes the microscopic scale; really, the single particles, how they behave," said study co-author Lukas Hennig , a doctoral student in advanced physics at Erlangen-Nürnberg.

Both theories assume Lorentz invariance to be true. But in extreme settings, such as the first moments after the Big Bang , the two theories don't mesh. That has fueled a decades-long hunt for a theory of quantum gravity that unites them. Some candidates, including versions of string theory and loop quantum gravity, suggest that space-time might have a hidden "grain" at the tiniest scales — and that Lorentz invariance, "one of the most basic assumptions we make about our universe, might be violated," Hennig said.

Any such violation would be extremely small. To spot it, physicists would need a probe that could travel long distances and barely interact with anything along the way. Enter the neutrino.

Neutrinos are nearly massless particles that pass through Earth every second and carry zero charge. They barely interact with anything and come in three types: electron, muon and tau neutrinos. As neutrinos travel, they morph from one type into another in a predictable pattern that physicists call neutrino oscillation.

If Lorentz invariance were broken, that oscillation would change, with the effect growing more pronounced the farther the neutrinos traveled. So the team focused on neutrinos created when cosmic rays slam into the atmosphere elsewhere on the globe before traveling up through the planet to the detector. Some of the tested neutrinos crossed the entire 7,900-mile (12,700 km) width of Earth.

ORCA is part of the KM3NeT neutrino telescope . Each of its detection units is anchored to the seabed and holds 18 glass spheres packed with 31 light sensors apiece. When a neutrino collides with a particle in the water, it produces a faint flash of blue light that the sensors catch. The many sensors in each sphere help the team pin down which direction the light came from, Domi said.

Earth itself serves as a filter. The researchers selected only particles traveling upward through the planet, and they were able to weed out the flood of other particles from the atmosphere that would otherwise swamp the signal. "Only the neutrinos can get through," Hennig said.

That setup differs from that of IceCube , the Nobel Prize-winning detector buried in Antarctic ice. "Ice scatters the light more than water, but on the other hand, water absorbs the light more than ice," Domi said, which changes how each team reconstructs a neutrino's energy and path.

The researchers used 5,828 neutrinos collected over about 17 months between 2020 and 2021. They found that the oscillations matched standard physics. That means if Lorentz violation exists, it must be weaker than the limits the team set.

Those limits matter for theorists. If a model "predicts a Lorentz invariance violation [stronger than the new limits], the data rule it out. In that case, you can be pretty sure that this model is not correct," Hennig said.

The team also set the first direct limits on a kind of violation that would treat muon neutrinos and tau neutrinos differently.

The detector's limits on several key measures are competitive with those from Japan's Super-Kamiokande , which used 12 years of data, and from IceCube, which used two years of data from its full array.

"I'm surprised that we have competitive results with only six detection units," Hennig said. Today, 44 units are in the water, and the collaboration plans to activate 108 by 2030.

The best tests may still lie ahead. Because Lorentz-violating effects grow with distance and energy, neutrinos from distant cosmic sources are "actually the best candidates to do this kind of research," Domi said. The team plans to repeat the search using ORCA's sister detector, ARCA (Astroparticle Research with Cosmics in the Abyss), which sits off the coast of Sicily and is designed to catch those high-energy cosmic travelers.

If space-time does have a grain, those particles may be among the first to feel it.

articles.title: NASA's Hubble studied 37 nearby dwarf galaxies and found they kept an average of just 11% of the oxygen made by their stars, leaving astronomers investigating where it went
articles.summary: Our cosmic neighbourhood is full of surprises, some you cannot even imagine.
articles.body: Our cosmic neighbourhood is full of surprises, some you cannot even imagine. In a paper published on Monday in The Astrophysical Journal, researchers using the Hubble Space Telescope studied 37 nearby dwarf galaxies and found that much of the oxygen they expected to find was missing. In fact, these galaxies retained just 11% of the oxygen their stars had produced over time. The rest appears to have been blown out into space, leaving astronomers with a rather interesting mystery to solve.What are dwarf galaxies?Dwarf galaxies are small galaxies containing anywhere between a few thousand and hundreds of millions of stars. This is considerably smaller than our Milky Way, which is estimated to contain around 100–400 billion stars. The Large Magellanic Cloud, a galaxy that closely orbits the Milky Way and contains billions of stars, is one example of a dwarf galaxy, although its classification has occasionally been debated.Despite their smaller size, dwarf galaxies are important to astronomers because they offer clues about how galaxies form and evolve. Their relatively low mass and weaker gravitational pull make them particularly interesting to study. Unlike larger galaxies, they can struggle to hold on to the gas and other material produced by their stars.Their evolution is also influenced by their surroundings. When dwarf galaxies pass close to larger galaxies, gravitational forces can pull at them, strip away their material and even disrupt their structure. Some eventually merge with larger galaxies, while others continue forming stars on their own.Astronomers classify dwarf galaxies into different types based on their shape, composition and activity. Some are rich in gas and continue producing new stars, while others have very little star formation left. Studying these differences helps scientists understand how galaxies change over billions of years.Where does oxygen in space come from?Oxygen isn't something we breathe in only on Earth. It is present throughout the universe, and stars are responsible for producing much of it.Stars are essentially enormous factories where nuclear reactions take place. Deep inside them, lighter elements combine to form heavier ones. Through these processes, stars produce elements such as carbon, oxygen, neon and magnesium. Oxygen, in particular, is created during the different stages of a star's life.When massive stars reach the end of their lives, they can explode in enormous blasts called supernovae. These explosions release energy and scatter the elements formed inside the stars into the surrounding space.In fact, many of the elements that make up our bodies, our planet and everything around us were created inside stars or during stellar explosions. In a way, we are all made up of star material.The case of the missing oxygenSince stars produce oxygen, scientists expected dwarf galaxies to contain a considerable amount of it. However, when researchers compared how much oxygen these galaxies should have produced with how much they could actually account for, the numbers did not add up.The team found that the 37 galaxies retained between 4% and 25% of the oxygen produced by their stars, with an average of just 11%. So, where did the remaining 89% go?Co-investigator Grace Telford, assistant professor in the Department of Physics and Astronomy at the University of Utah, explained that oxygen must have been inside these galaxies at some point because their stars produced it. For it to be missing now, it must have been pushed out. This requires enormous amounts of energy, which can come from massive stars and supernova explosions.Where did the oxygen go?To investigate, researchers studied the galaxies as part of the Galaxies Losing Oxygen via Winds (GLOW) project, funded by NASA and the National Science Foundation. They used archival observations from Hubble to study individual stars and understand the galaxies' star formation histories. Data from NASA's retired Spitzer Space Telescope and ground-based radio telescopes, including the Very Large Array and the Australian Telescope Compact Array, helped them examine the gas and other material within these galaxies.The researchers found that powerful stellar explosions can generate enormous outflows of gas called galactic winds. These winds carry oxygen-rich material away from the galaxies and into the space between them. According to the study, galactic winds are much more effective at removing oxygen from low-mass galaxies than current scientific models had predicted.This is largely because dwarf galaxies have relatively weak gravity. Think of trying to hold on to a balloon in a strong gust of wind. A larger galaxy has a stronger gravitational pull, making it better equipped to hold on to its material. A dwarf galaxy, on the other hand, struggles to keep the gas produced by its stars from escaping.However, scientists have not yet established exactly where all the missing oxygen ends up. Some of it could remain in the diffuse clouds of gas surrounding galaxies, known as the circumgalactic medium, while the rest may have travelled much farther into the space between galaxies.Why does this discovery matter?Oxygen is the third most abundant element in the universe, after hydrogen and helium. It is also relatively easy for astronomers to detect and measure, making it a useful marker for understanding how elements are distributed across galaxies.When stars produce elements and release them into space, they enrich the universe with the ingredients needed to form new stars and planets. By tracing oxygen, scientists can understand how galaxies evolve and how material travels beyond their boundaries into the wider universe.The discovery also suggests that existing computer simulations may have underestimated how efficiently galactic winds remove material from smaller galaxies. Understanding this process could help astronomers build more accurate models of how galaxies develop over time.The investigation is far from over. Researchers hope to study even smaller and fainter galaxies using NASA's Nancy Grace Roman Space Telescope, alongside further observations from Hubble and the James Webb Space Telescope. They also plan to examine individual massive stars to understand how they produce oxygen and help drive it out of their host galaxies.For now, the missing oxygen remains a cosmic mystery. Scientists know that these tiny galaxies are producing it, and that much of it is escaping. The next challenge is to find out just how far it has travelled.

articles.title: Blue Origin’s next launch now won’t happen until 2027
articles.summary: Blue Origin plans to do its next New Glenn rocket launch in January 2027, according to a memo reportedly sent by CEO Dave Limp to staff.
articles.body: Blue Origin plans to do its next New Glenn rocket launch in January 2027, according to CNBC and the Financial Times, which cite a memo from CEO Dave Limp sent to staff. The new timeline follows a May launchpad explosion that damaged Blue Origin’s New Glenn launchpad ahead of a flight that would have brought Amazon Leo satellites into space. In October, Blue Origin founder Jeff Bezos told Fox News that the company was aiming for a December New Glenn launch, joking that it could be “probably December 31st.” The new, revised launch window is “about 10 days later than Blue Origin’s earlier launch target,” CNBC reports. Limp also reportedly cited bad weather as having an effect on the launchpad rebuilding process. “This small adjustment doesn’t diminish what we’ve accomplished or the importance of the work still ahead,” Limp wrote in his memo, per CNBC and the FT. “Returning New Glenn to flight remains our top priority — it’s worth it.”

articles.title: World First: Underwater Volcano Off US Coast Generates Net-Positive Electricity
articles.summary: Volcanic heat, electricity to spare.
articles.body:
An engineering team lowered a generator to the ocean floor and ran it using heat from an underwater volcano. They wanted to find out whether it could produce more electricity than it needed to operate.

For 8.7 seconds, the system did just that.

Seattle-based Endurance Energy announced the results of its Adélie experiment on October 19 in a company press release .

The test took place at Axial Seamount, an underwater volcano about 480 kilometers (300 miles) off Oregon. Here, hot springs emerge from the seabed roughly 1,500 meters (5,000 feet) below the ocean's surface.

The water gets its heat from molten rock beneath the volcano. Seawater seeps into cracks in the seabed, heats up underground, and flows back into the ocean through openings called hydrothermal vents .

Endurance's engineers set out to capture some of that heat. On land, geothermal power plants already use hot water or steam from underground to generate electricity. Heat drives a spinning machine called a turbine, which turns a generator. This energy source doesn't depend on sunshine or wind.

To make it work on the seabed, the team first needed enough hot water flowing through its equipment. Engineers drilled a well extending 16 meters (52 feet) beneath the ocean floor, installed a pipe inside it, and cemented it in place.

Water emerged at about 260 °C (500 °F), but its flow was too restricted to run the generator.

The engineers connected Adélie to a nearby natural vent. Heat for the successful test therefore came from water already flowing out of the seabed.

During the September 27 experiment, that water was approximately 281 °C (538 °F). High pressure at this depth allows water to remain liquid well above its surface boiling temperature of 100 °C (212 °F).

As the system ran, its turbine reached approximately 26,000 revolutions per minute.

The team controlled the equipment from Seattle. Scientists already monitor the active underwater volcano using instruments connected to shore.

An existing undersea cable network called the Regional Cabled Array , operated by the University of Washington, provided the connection for Endurance's experiment.

The pumps and other components also consumed electricity. After subtracting that demand, the company's press release reported a median surplus of about 2 kilowatts during the 8.7-second interval, with a peak of 16.5 kilowatts.

Researchers have generated electricity from seafloor vents before. In a study published in Applied Energy in 2016 , a Chinese team described a device that converted the temperature difference between hot vent water and cold seawater into electricity.

The device continuously produced 2.6–3.9 watts during its field test and powered a data logger and an LED lamp.

Endurance's longer-term goal is to supply customers on land.

The company says its first commercial project is being developed in Tonga, a Pacific island nation whose electricity grid relies largely on imported diesel. It is targeting first power in 2027.

Reaching that goal will require much longer operation. Adélie's run stopped when a safety system protecting its battery from excessive current activated. About 10 minutes later, a pump power cable failed during a restart attempt.

"Gentoo, Endurance's next 100kW test generator, is an upgraded Adélie. It deploys this winter and targets higher power and longer runs," Endurance founder and CEO Andrew Redd told ScienceAlert.

Redd said the updated equipment will address the battery protection and pump cable problems encountered during the test.

"Endurance has a new drill coming online next year which will reach 500m depth at maximum," Redd said.

That's about 1,640 feet, compared with the current drill's 80-meter (260-foot) maximum. The company expects deeper wells to provide greater water flow.

Redd said the team still needs to achieve sustained generation from a drilled well and develop equipment that operates reliably for months or years.

These figures describe electricity production during operation. They don't account for the energy spent on shipping, drilling, and installation. The measurements come from Endurance, and its announcement includes no peer-reviewed paper reporting the results.

Environmental questions also remain. Microbes around vents use chemicals for energy, and tubeworms and other animals depend on those microbes .

Endurance says it chose a drilling location away from the vent chimneys and nearby animals. Its monitoring found no notable change in the life around the site, the company reported.

According to the announcement, more than 40 water, rock, and mineral samples were sent to independent laboratories for analysis. Longer-term effects remain to be established.

"We recognize that larger systems running continuously over years could affect the surrounding water column, biological communities and seafloor habitat," Redd said.

The company is working with independent researchers on further analysis and studies, Redd added.

The experiment showed that the generator could briefly produce more electricity than it consumed. The next test is whether it can keep running. Longer deployments will also help establish how it affects the surrounding ocean .

articles.title: T-Mobile owner on Elon Musk launching a wireless carrier: ‘Welcome to the party’
articles.summary: Deutsche Telekom CEO Tim Höttges is casting doubt on SpaceX’s ambitions to make Starlink Mobile a major US mobile carrier, saying it could cost at least $200 billion to pull off.
articles.body: The head of T-Mobile’s parent company is casting doubt on SpaceX’s plans to make Starlink Mobile a “major” carrier in the US. During an earnings call on Thursday, Deutsche Telekom CEO Tim Höttges says he takes the Elon Musk-owned company “super serious,” but that it will cost at least $200 billion to pull off: > He [Musk] has now bought 76 megahertz of spectrum. By the way, we have 400. So if you now say he can buy the spectrum prospectively, do your math. These are kind of triple-digit billions which are needed to gain the spectrum position. If he has the money, go for it. Then he has to build a network. I can tell you, we have 85,000 towers. No, he can rent towers, no question. But this is another $20 to $30 billion which are required. > Put antennas on it. You can buy antennas… and you can get [them] maybe even in a cheaper way, or you construct it in a new way, but you need money for that. So therefore, my assessment is that SpaceX at least — if they want to play in that industry — needs at least minimum $200 billion. But even beyond that, to play in an industry which we have, let’s say, professionalized over the last 20 years — okay, welcome to the party. Last month, SpaceX laid out its plans for Starlink Mobile to compete against T-Mobile, AT&T, and Verizon by using a combination of direct-to-cell satellites and a terrestrial network. One recent report suggests that SpaceX could tap into 80,000 cell towers throughout the US, while another indicates that Musk was in talks to acquire Boost Mobile. This week, Qualcomm announced that SpaceX will use its cellular infrastructure technology to support Starlink Mobile’s network buildout. [Media: At the same time, Höttges is aware of the potential threat Starlink Mobile could pose to the mobile industry by creating a “new” type of service. “He [Musk] has chipsets, he has data centers, he has AI, he has satellites… He will go as well for maybe integrating social media or at least agent models into his service. So he is creating a new way of communication services,” Höttges says. “That is why I’m saying I take that super serious because I was witnessing what happened to the car industry. They were ignoring it for too long, and we have to face the situation. But it’s not a free lunch. And you see that with Tesla as well in the car industry.”

articles.title: US wildlife teams surveyed six offshore islands for invasive species, finding rats on five and iguanas on one; the results will guide future work to protect nesting seabirds
articles.summary: Islands are often considered safe havens for wildlife, away from the rushing development of humanity, particularly for seabirds that depend on remote and
articles.body: Islands are often considered safe havens for wildlife, away from the rushing development of humanity, particularly for seabirds that depend on remote and undisturbed locations to lay their eggs and raise their young. However, humans cannot take a rest; human activities have led to the introduction of non-native invasive species to the islands. These animal species can disturb the balance, putting species that have depended on these habitats for generations at risk. Now, a wildlife assessment in the Caribbean has revealed the presence of invasive animals on several small islands, highlighting the challenges conservationists face in protecting these nesting grounds.The assessment was carried out across six offshore cays managed by Virgin Islands National Park in the U.S. Virgin Islands. Preliminary findings recorded black rats on five of the islands and green iguanas on one, giving wildlife teams a better understanding of the threats that could affect local seabird populations.The project was led by the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service's Caribbean Coastal Program in partnership with Island Conservation, a nonprofit organisation that works to restore island ecosystems by removing invasive species. The findings will help conservation partners decide what steps are needed to protect the islands and make them suitable for seabirds to return.Why invasive rats are a concern for Caribbean seabirdsOffshore cays within Virgin Islands National Park have historically supported seabird colonies, providing important nesting grounds for species such as the red-billed tropicbird, roseate tern and laughing gull. These birds depend on suitable nesting habitats to reproduce, but invasive predators can make these locations increasingly difficult to use, especially rats. People from New York would know what is being talked about.Black rats are particularly concerning because they prey on seabird eggs and chicks. Their presence can lead to failed nesting attempts and contribute to declining bird populations. On small islands, where seabirds may have few alternative nesting locations, the introduction of such predators can have serious consequences for local wildlife.The green iguana, another non-native species, although it looks harmless and exotic, is a threat to local diversity. The survey’s results are still being studied, and conservation teams may conduct additional assessments to understand the situation more completely.A collaborative effort to assess the islandsThe project received its first funding in 2024. For the assessment, the team also looked at older seabird survey records and carried out fieldwork in December 2025. The U.S. Virgin Islands Division of Fish and Wildlife shared data from its annual seabird surveys around St. John, while biologists from the Coastal Program, national park staff and Friends of the Virgin Islands National Park helped with the planning and fieldwork.Friends of the Virgin Islands National Park also provided additional funding for the project, which brought together several organisations to study the islands and identify where conservation work may be needed.What happens next?The survey has given the park a better idea of which invasive animals are present on the six cays and where work may be needed. The next step could involve removing rats and iguanas from the islands and making sure they do not return, so that seabirds can nest there without the same threats.Conservation teams may also use sound-attraction devices to bring seabirds back to suitable nesting sites. These devices play recordings of seabird calls, which can encourage birds to settle and form colonies in an area.A similar approach has been used on Desecheo Island National Wildlife Refuge in Puerto Rico. The work in the U.S. Virgin Islands could help give the seabirds that once nested on these small islands a safer place to return to.While approaches can be many, they are not always solutions. Human intervention has led to the demise of many species, and the dodo bird speaks for itself. Its extinction is a reminder of how easily human activities can disturb an island ecosystem and put an entire species at risk. The six cays in the U.S. Virgin Islands are now facing their own conservation challenges, and the hope is that timely efforts will protect their native seabirds before history repeats itself.

articles.title: Cientistas encontram evidência mais antiga do uso de maconha em túmulo de 2.800 anos na Sibéria | G1
articles.body:
Uma trança de cabelo humano preservada, datada de cerca de 2.800 anos atrás, no sítio arqueológico de um antigo túmulo cita, no Vale dos Czares, República de Tuva, sul da Sibéria , Rússia, nesta imagem divulgada em 5 de novembro de 2026 — Foto: REUTERS

Um túmulo siberiano da antiga cultura cita, datado de 2.800 anos atrás , revelou a evidência mais antiga conhecida do uso da cannabis por seus efeitos psicoativos , com cientistas encontrando sementes da planta entre os objetos funerários e cabelos humanos que apresentavam suas marcas químicas dentro do túmulo.

Pesquisadores afirmaram que as evidências foram desenterradas em uma estrutura funerária monumental, com cerca de 140 metros de diâmetro , localizada no Vale de Uyuk, na remota República de Tuva, na Rússia.

O túmulo, no sul da Sibéria, era o local de descanso final de membros de alto escalão da sociedade cita, conhecida por sua expertise em guerra a cavalo e ourivesaria, além de seu estilo de vida relativamente nômade nas estepes da Eurásia.

A cannabis é uma planta versátil que vem sendo utilizada e domesticada há milhares de anos, não apenas para fins psicoativos -- para “ ficar chapado ” --, mas também pela produção de fibras e sementes oleaginosas .

É uma das substâncias intoxicantes mais consumidas atualmente. No entanto, compreender a história de seu uso psicoativo tem sido difícil devido à natureza perecível dos restos da planta.

“Há muita especulação sobre o uso de drogas psicoativas no passado, mas muito raramente encontramos evidências concretas e podemos realmente confirmar que uma planta foi consumida para esse fim”, disse o arqueólogo Gino Caspari, da Universidade de Berna, na Suíça, e do Instituto Max Planck de Geoantropologia, na Alemanha, que liderou o estudo publicado na revista Science.

“A razão para isso é que matéria vegetal e tecido mole humano raramente sobrevivem, e ainda mais raro é que sejam preservados no mesmo contexto. Nosso estudo mostra a evidência direta mais antiga do consumo psicoativo de cannabis”, disse Caspari.

Essa conclusão é reforçada pelo fato de que a descoberta foi feita em um sítio funerário e está associada a elaborados rituais de sepultamento.

O local antecede as evidências mais antigas até então conhecidas, datadas do primeiro milênio a.C. , de uso da cannabis para alterar a consciência, como vestígios de instrumentos usados para queimá-la encontrados no Oriente Médio e nas montanhas Pamir, na Ásia Central.

Os pesquisadores recuperaram mais de 1.400 sementes de cannabis associadas a sepultamentos dentro do túmulo siberiano e utilizaram uma técnica científica de datação para determinar que são do início do século 8 a.C .

“Objetos de valor no mundo dos vivos costumavam ser incluídos no contexto funerário como oferendas nesta região”, disse Caspari.

A análise química das tranças de cabelo dos corpos de diversas pessoas encontradas na câmara funerária central identificou assinaturas químicas consistentes com o THC , composto psicoativo da cannabis, e traços de canabinol, um composto relacionado ao THC .

“O corpo humano realmente produz moléculas relacionadas à cannabis, como o THC e o CBD, no cabelo. É assim que funcionam os testes de drogas”, disse Caspari.

“Não podemos afirmar com certeza como eles consumiam a substância com base apenas no cabelo, mas, considerando evidências posteriores na região, parece provável que ela fosse inalada.”

O monte funerário foi construído com troncos de lariço e argila , e todo o conjunto está envolto por milhares de toneladas de pedras. Os pesquisadores recuperaram, no interior, itens trabalhados em um estilo artístico chamado “ estilo animal cita ”, assim como vários objetos incomuns de ouro.

Na superfície do monte funerário, os citas aparentemente realizavam sacrifícios de animais envolvendo dezenas de cavalos e, provavelmente, também de pessoas, disse Caspari, considerando os ossos humanos dispersos encontrados entre os vestígios.

"Encontrar cannabis em uma grande sepultura já indica que ela deve ser interpretada em um contexto ritual. Constatamos que tanto sacrifícios de animais quanto de seres humanos podem ter sido dispostos na superfície do monte na forma de uma espécie de cavalgada espectral. Sustentados por estacas, os cavalos e cavaleiros mortos formariam uma demonstração de poder social extremo dentro das comunidades das estepes", disse Caspari.

Os citas entraram em contato com ricas culturas de sua época, incluindo a Grécia antiga, conforme documentado pelo historiador Heródoto, do século 5 a.C.

“Heródoto descreveu o ritual da cavalgada espectral, mas sempre tivemos certa hesitação em acreditar em seus escritos, já que ele tende a se perder no fantástico.

Depois de encontrar os restos mortais no sul da Sibéria, sabemos que pelo menos algumas de suas descrições sobre os povos das estepes continham alguma verdade”, disse Caspari.

As sementes descobertas no local estavam em bom estado de conservação .

“É aqui que a coisa fica ainda mais empolgante. Começamos a sequenciar algumas das sementes e encontramos DNA muito bem preservado”, disse Caspari.

“Isso é ainda mais raro do que encontrar os próprios restos de plantas, e atualmente é o DNA de cannabis mais antigo conhecido. Acho que, nos próximos anos, seremos capazes de acrescentar detalhes e reescrever parcialmente a história da domesticação dessa importante cultura.”

articles.title: Scientists examining dinosaur fossils report evidence of preserved red blood cells and collagen amino acids, a finding led by Curtin University that could change how researchers investigate ancient biological material
articles.summary: Time has a way of taking almost everything away. Bodies decay. Tissues disappear, and even bones gradually change as millions of years pass.
articles.body: Time has a way of taking almost everything away. Bodies decay. Tissues disappear, and even bones gradually change as millions of years pass. Out of the excruciating cycle of time, nature sometimes decides to find a loophole by preserving a few traces for us to find and know that we were not the only ones and we won't be. One day, we find something that makes us wonder how that's even possible, and the next, nature throws even bigger mind-boggling stuff at us. Something similar happened with a group of palaeontologists when they found dinosaur blood.When we think of dinosaur fossils, we usually imagine enormous skeletons, sharp teeth and footprints preserved in rocks for millions of years. But what if I told you that some fossils may hold traces of something far more delicate? In a study led by researchers at Curtin University, scientists examined a 115-million-year-old dinosaur fossil and reported evidence of structures resembling red blood cells, along with collagen-related molecules. The findings offer a rare glimpse into the biological material that may survive inside fossils long after an animal's death.The findings were published in a study in the journal Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences (PNAS), titled ‘Heme signatures in mineralised red blood cells within vascular canals of a 115-million-year-old dinosaur bone’.The discovery of traces of dinosaur bloodThe research was led by Kliti Grice of Curtin University, along with an international team of scientists. They were examining the limb bones of Aratasaurus museunacionali, a theropod dinosaur that lived in what is now northeastern Brazil around 115 million years ago. The fossil bones, which were discovered in a Brazilian mine in 2008, held something researchers did not expect to find.While examining the samples, scientists noticed tiny, oval-shaped structures inside the vascular canals of the bones. These canals are the pathways through which blood vessels once passed. The structures appeared similar to red blood cells, but the researchers needed more than their appearance to establish what they were.The team therefore used several advanced chemical and imaging techniques to investigate them. Using high-performance liquid chromatography-mass spectrometry, researchers identified heme B and its altered forms in the bone extracts. Heme is an iron-containing molecule found in haemoglobin, the protein that allows red blood cells to transport oxygen throughout the body.Further analysis using Raman spectroscopy and transmission electron microscopy revealed chemical signatures associated with heme inside the structures, along with elements such as iron, nitrogen and carbon. Researchers also identified the mineral hausmannite, which may have helped stabilise the structures and preserve the biological traces over millions of years.Along with blood, the team also detected traces of collagen in the fossil. Together, these findings provide evidence of blood-derived molecules and collagen-related material surviving in a dinosaur fossil for approximately 115 million years.But the question still remains: how exactly did the blood survive for 115 million years?How did dinosaur blood survive for 115 million years?Normally, blood cells and other soft tissues begin breaking down soon after an animal dies. Microorganisms, oxygen and natural chemical processes gradually decompose these delicate structures, making their preservation over millions of years extremely difficult.Researchers believe the answer could lie in the environment in which the dinosaur died and was eventually buried. According to the study, the animal may have been rapidly buried in a low-oxygen environment rich in microbial mats. These are thin layers of microorganisms, including bacteria and archaea, that commonly develop in shallow-water environments. Such conditions may have slowed normal decomposition and created an environment favourable for the preservation of delicate biological structures.However, the researchers believe another factor played an equally important role. They found that the cell-like structures were mineralised with hausmannite, a manganese oxide mineral. This mineral may have acted like a protective casing, helping stabilise the microscopic structures and their associated chemical components before they could completely break down.In other words, the researchers believe that a combination of favourable burial conditions and early mineralisation of the fossil may have helped preserve traces of biological material that would normally disappear. Beyond explaining how these traces survived for millions of years, the discovery unravels something more fundamental. Until now, our understanding of these creatures came from bones, teeth and fossilised footprints. However, finding blood-derived molecules and collagen-related material offers researchers a completely new way to look at them, potentially revealing details that skeletal remains alone could not tell us. It also raises the possibility that fossils may hold far more biological information than scientists have been able to uncover so far.

articles.title: Archaeologists studying an ancient Spanish copper mine uncovered stone tools and new evidence of Bronze Age production; the findings suggest metal from Iberia may have travelled as far north as Scandinavia
articles.summary: Have you ever wondered where the things our ancestors used came from?
articles.body: Have you ever wondered where the things our ancestors used came from? Today, we can order almost anything from anywhere in the world, and a product can travel thousands of kilometres before reaching our doorstep. But what about people who lived thousands of years ago? How did they find the materials they needed, and did they really have connections with communities living far away? These questions have fascinated historians and archaeologists for generations, and sometimes, a discovery at a seemingly ordinary location can tell us much more about how people lived and interacted with one another.Copper was one such material that changed the course of human history. During the Bronze Age, people mixed copper with tin to produce bronze, which was then used to make tools, weapons and ornaments. But copper was not available everywhere, and communities often had to depend on other regions to obtain it. Now, a study of an ancient copper mine in southern Spain has offered new clues about how far this metal may have travelled, with evidence suggesting that some of it could have reached Scandinavia, thousands of kilometres away.The research focuses on Las Minillas, an ancient copper mine in the Badajoz region of southern Spain. Archaeologists combined excavations, underground surveys and radiocarbon dating to understand how the mine was used during the Bronze Age. Their findings, published in the journal Antiquity, suggest that Las Minillas was part of a much wider network of prehistoric mining sites across the Iberian Peninsula.What did archaeologists find at the ancient copper mine?One of the most interesting discoveries at Las Minillas was the number of stone tools left behind by the people who worked there. Researchers recovered hundreds of tools, including 735 grooved stone hammers that were likely used to break and extract copper-bearing rock. They also found fragments of handmade pottery, offering further clues about the people who worked at the site.The team collected charcoal samples from the mine and obtained 17 additional radiocarbon dates, placing its activity between approximately 1350 and 750 BC. The evidence suggests that copper production at Las Minillas was active between around 1300 and 800/700 BC, making it the largest securely dated Late Bronze Age copper mine excavated in Iberia so far.Interestingly, the mine was not necessarily working in isolation. Researchers identified 84 mining sites as part of a wider network stretching from southern Portugal to southeastern Spain. However, the exact extent of this network and whether all these locations were active at the same time remain unclear.Did copper from Spain reach Scandinavia?The discovery becomes even more interesting when we look at the possible journey of the copper extracted from these mines. During the Bronze Age, different communities depended on the exchange of raw materials, and copper was an important part of this trade. Since not every region had its own copper deposits, the metal could travel between communities before being turned into objects used in everyday life.To understand where the copper may have gone, researchers compared the chemical composition and lead-isotope signatures of ores and metalworking remains from Las Minillas with existing records of Bronze Age objects. Lead-isotope analysis helps archaeologists study the geological origins of metals and compare them with known mining regions.The comparison revealed that 11 Scandinavian bronze objects had signatures consistent with copper from Las Minillas. This suggests that metal extracted in southern Spain may have travelled much farther north than the mine itself, potentially through several communities and trading networks.However, this does not mean that copper was transported directly from Spain to Scandinavia. It may have changed hands several times before reaching its final destination. The findings instead offer evidence of the connections that existed between distant parts of Europe during the Bronze Age.How Iberia may have become an important copper supplierFor a long time, archaeological research into Bronze Age copper production in Europe has focused on well-known mining regions such as Wales and the Austrian Alps. The Mitterberg mining district in Austria, for instance, was a major supplier of copper to Central Europe during the Middle Bronze Age. Mines in Wales and the Italian Alps also played an important role in supplying metal to other regions.However, the production at some of these older mining centres began to decline around the middle of the second millennium BC. Researchers suggest that southern Iberia may have become a more important source of copper during the Late Bronze Age, particularly from around 1300/1200 BC.The study estimates that Las Minillas may have produced between 49 and 738 tonnes of copper, although the researchers favour a more cautious estimate of around 197 tonnes. They also suggest that copper from southern Iberia could have reached distant markets through maritime trade routes along the Atlantic coast.There is still much that researchers do not know. Several ancient mines across the Iberian Peninsula remain unexplored or have not been reliably dated, making it difficult to establish how extensive the mining network really was. Further research could help determine whether these sites formed part of a large, active copper-producing region or operated at different periods.What makes Las Minillas particularly interesting is that it offers a glimpse into a world where communities separated by thousands of kilometres may have been connected through something as ordinary as metal. The copper extracted from these Spanish mines was not just a resource for the people who worked there; it may have travelled across Europe, finding its way into objects used by people who would never have known where it came from.

articles.title: For years, floods swallowed streets and threatened homes, then a Philippine fishing village used bamboo, oyster shells and coconut waste to make a natural coastal defence that has prevented flooding for two years
articles.summary: For years, residents of Pamarawan, a small fishing village on the edge of Manila Bay in the Philippines, watched floodwaters enter their streets and
articles.body: For years, residents of Pamarawan, a small fishing village on the edge of Manila Bay in the Philippines, watched floodwaters enter their streets and threaten homes whenever strong monsoon winds or typhoons sent waves crashing towards the coast. Even a concrete breakwater, standing up to four metres high, was not enough to keep the water out. During storms, waves would rise almost a metre above the barrier, directly hitting houses built beside it.But the village's approach to protecting itself has taken an unusual turn. Instead of depending only on more concrete walls, Pamarawan has begun using bamboo poles, discarded oyster shells and coconut husks to create a nature-based coastal defence system. The initiative is designed not only to weaken incoming waves but also to trap sediment, encourage mangrove growth and help restore marine habitats.According to a report by Mongabay, local officials say the village has gone almost two years without flooding since the project began. They also say Pamarawan escaped the severe flooding that affected neighbouring communities in August this year, when several parts of Bulacan province were inundated for weeks.Bamboo, oyster shells and coconut husks protecting the villageThe project covers approximately 14 hectares (35 acres) of coastal waters around Pamarawan, a low-lying barangay, or village, in Malolos City, Bulacan province. Its central feature is a network of interconnected bamboo structures known as bamboo cribs. These structures work as breakwaters, reducing the energy of waves before they reach the shoreline. They also act as sediment traps, allowing mud and sand carried by the water to settle instead of being washed away.Discarded oyster shells have been placed inside coconut-husk mesh bags, locally referred to as cocomesh. These bags form another part of the coastal defence system, helping weaken waves while creating conditions that could support the restoration of oyster reefs.The project is designed to work with natural coastal processes rather than simply block the sea with a hard barrier. As sediment accumulates around the bamboo structures, the seabed is expected to rise gradually. Once it reaches a suitable level, mangroves can be planted, creating another layer of natural protection against waves and storm surges.According to barangay councilor Ferdinand Cruz, sediment has already accumulated to approximately 0.3 metres (one foot) in some areas. Local officials expect that parts of the seabed could become suitable for mangrove planting within two years.A village that lost its natural protectionPamarawan's flooding problem is linked to several environmental pressures. The area experiences strong waves during the southwest monsoon, locally known as habagat, while typhoons and high tides further increase the risk of coastal inundation. Rising sea levels and land subsidence, partly associated with excessive groundwater extraction, have also worsened flooding in low-lying parts of North Manila Bay.The village once had thick mangrove forests that helped absorb wave energy and protect homes. But these natural barriers disappeared as coastal areas across Bulacan were converted for fishponds and land reclamation. Between 1990 and 2002, the province lost 52.9% of its mangrove forests, according to figures cited by Mongabay.Pamarawan barangay secretary Roldan Dayao recalled how the loss of mangroves changed the village's relationship with the sea. "They could block the big waves," he said, referring to the mangroves. "But when our mangroves disappeared, the water began entering our barangay." The new project aims to restore some of that lost protection by creating conditions in which mangroves and oyster reefs can eventually return.Almost two years without floodingDayao told Mongabay that Pamarawan had not experienced flooding for almost two years since the nature-based project began. Cruz also said the village escaped the severe flooding that affected nearby communities in August 2026. According to the report, the flooding in Bulacan lasted for weeks, killed 15 people and prompted the provincial government to declare a state of calamity."It rained almost every day, and there was habagat, but we did not experience flooding," Cruz said. He added that some neighbouring communities at higher elevations were submerged, with water reaching halfway up houses and, in some cases, almost covering their roofs.Residents have also noticed that the bamboo structures are attracting marine life, including shrimps, crabs and oysters, which local fishers are allowed to collect. They have reported that less waste from Manila Bay is reaching the shoreline.Could this approach work elsewhere?The pilot project was developed by Dutch engineering firm Haskoning and approved by Malolos Mayor Christian Natividad in 2023. Construction began in 2024, with the city government allocating 130 million Philippine pesos (approximately $2 million) towards the initiative. The Netherlands Enterprise Agency supported the detailed engineering design. The project has attracted attention from Philippine authorities as a possible model for other flood-prone coastal communities. In September 2026, Department of Public Works and Highways Secretary Vince Dizon praised the initiative and discussed the possibility of replicating its approach in other parts of North Manila Bay.The Philippine Information Agency reported in October that the project was also being discussed as an example of nature-based flood protection during an ASEAN-Netherlands cross-learning workshop. However, Haskoning has cautioned against copying the design without considering local conditions. Each coastline has different ecological, geological and social characteristics, meaning flood protection measures must be adapted to the location.

articles.title: Cae en la Tierra un telescopio de la NASA: se lanzó en 2004 y estudiaba las explosiones más potentes del universo
articles.standfirst: En agosto había fracasado un intento de alargar su vida útil
articles.summary: En agosto había fracasado un intento de alargar su vida útil
articles.body: Tras más de 20 años, un telescopio de la NASA ha caído en la Tierra, tal y como ha confirmado la Fuerza Espacial de Estados Unidos. Su función había sido la de detectar y estudiar las explosiones de rayos gamma, consideradas las más potentes del universo. Como se preveía inicialmente, la mayor parte del artefacto se ha desintegrado en su entrada a la atmósfera de nuestro planeta. El comunicado difundido explica que se trata del telescopio Swift, de casi 1.500 kilogramos y que se movía en una órbita por debajo de los 375 kilómetros. La duda de los expertos respecto al aparato era qué iba a pasar con el resto, en concreto dónde iba a impactar. Para ello, el momento de la reentrada era crucial. Finalmente, los restos han caído sobre el norte de la isla de Sumatra después de 22 años recogiendo datos y tras lograr sobrevivir por mucho su vida útil prevista y tras enviar datos de más de 2.000 explosiones. Para alargar su tiempo de uso, el pasado mes de agosto la NASA puso en marcha un arriesgado plan: lanzó un robot motorizado que tenía como objetivo alejar al aparato de la Tierra. Sin embargo, esta maniobra fracasó y obligó a la agencia a seguir un nuevo rumbo y analizar su caída, que se ha acelerado debido a una tormenta solar el pasado fin de semana. El telescopio Swift se componía de tres aparatos, destacando el primero por su capacidad para orientarse, girar y moverse en pocos segundos y apuntar a la explosión con una alta precisión. Su trabajo ha servido para el estudio de muchos astrónomos, que han encargado al Swift una gran cantidad de observaciones a lo largo de los últimos 22 años que ha estado activo.

articles.title: For decades, physicists assumed black holes can merge but cannot split; new calculations suggest a black hole spinning near its maximum speed might break in two, though nobody has ever observed it happening.
articles.summary: Black holes are mysteriously the most fascinating and dreadful part of the universe. Scientists have been trying to know how they work.
articles.body: Black holes are mysteriously the most fascinating and dreadful part of the universe. Scientists have been trying to know how they work. Not until very recently did scientists even know what they looked like. It was only on April 10, 2019, that the first image of a black hole's shadow was captured by the Event Horizon Telescope. Before that, they just assumed based on mathematical calculations. The closest representation came not from a lab but from the movie Interstellar, where they created the imagery of a black hole on screen using VFX and CGI. It's another fascinating aspect of science: how you can know what something might look like based on mathematical calculations.There have been many theories, many assumptions and ideas surrounding black holes. Each day, we find something new, which leads us into a greater depth of mystery. For decades, scientists only knew that black holes could merge. With their great gravitational force, which even prevents light from escaping, two black holes can attract each other and become one. But the new study says something else. A new theoretical study suggests that this extraordinary possibility is extremely rare even theoretically, although it is possible under extreme conditions.The research, published in Physical Review D under the title "When Black Holes Admit Pair-of-pants Topologies", examines the physical laws that keep a black hole intact and whether certain circumstances could allow it to break apart.Why do scientists believe black holes cannot split?To understand the unusual possibility, we first have to understand how these massive holes are formed. A black hole is a region of space where gravity becomes so powerful that nothing, not even light, can escape once it crosses a boundary known as the event horizon. According to Einstein's theory of general relativity, the event horizon marks the point beyond which our usual understanding of space and time changes dramatically.However, gravity is not the only reason scientists have long considered black hole splitting impossible. Another important concept is entropy, which is closely related to the second law of thermodynamics. In simple terms, entropy is a measure of how many possible microscopic arrangements a physical system can have. Black holes also possess entropy, which is related to the surface area of their event horizons.According to the area theorem proposed by physicist Stephen Hawking, the total surface area of black hole event horizons cannot decrease in a classical physical process, assuming certain conditions hold. When two black holes merge, their combined event horizon can form a larger one, satisfying this principle. However, if one black hole were to split into two smaller ones, the total area of the resulting event horizons would generally be smaller than that of the original black hole. This would go against the area theorem, making such a process theoretically unfavourable.This is why scientists have traditionally considered black holes capable of merging but not splitting. However, the new research explores whether an extremely rapidly rotating black hole could present an exception to this long-standing understanding.How could a rapidly spinning black hole split into two?This is where the new research gets particularly interesting. The researchers suggest that a black hole spinning close to its maximum possible speed could behave differently from what scientists have traditionally expected. Rotation plays an important role in determining the physical properties of a black hole, including its mass, angular momentum and event horizon.The study examines whether this extreme rotation could allow a black hole to overcome the restrictions that ordinarily prevent it from splitting. According to the researchers' calculations, under very specific conditions, a rapidly spinning black hole could theoretically divide into two smaller black holes without violating the underlying physical principles considered in the study.The researchers describe this unusual possibility through something called a pair-of-pants topology. Imagine the shape of a pair of trousers: a single upper section branching into two separate legs. In a similar way, the event horizon of the original black hole would branch into two separate horizons, each belonging to a smaller black hole.However, this does not mean that every rapidly spinning black hole is capable of splitting. The conditions are extremely restrictive, and the resulting black holes would also need to move far enough apart to avoid merging again. The possibility remains theoretical, and no such event has ever been observed.While the possibility remains far from being observed, at least for now, the study does challenge the long-held assumptions about black holes and reminds us that even the most extreme objects in the universe may still hold surprises.
