articles.title: Scientists tracked 356 Burmese pythons in Florida for 8 years and uncovered a surprising winter habit, with some invasive snakes climbing trees as high as 7 metres above the ground
articles.summary: Florida’s invasive Burmese pythons are known for moving through wetlands and dense vegetation, but new research has revealed that some also spend time
articles.body: Florida’s invasive Burmese pythons are known for moving through wetlands and dense vegetation, but new research has revealed that some also spend time high above the ground. Scientists tracking 356 snakes in Big Cypress National Preserve over eight years recorded occasional tree-climbing behaviour, with one adult male reaching a height of seven metres. The findings show that these movements are more common during the cooler winter months, when pythons may use branches to bask and absorb heat. The discovery offers wildlife managers fresh information about the snakes’ movements and raises questions about their possible encounters with native birds.How scientists tracked 356 Burmese pythons in FloridaBurmese pythons have established themselves across much of southern Florida, where they occupy a range of natural environments. Their ability to live in different habitats has made them difficult to monitor, and understanding where they spend their time remains a persistent problem for wildlife managers. To examine their movements more closely, scientists from the US Geological Survey (USGS) and collaborating institutions followed 356 snakes in Big Cypress National Preserve. The tracking work took place between 2017 and 2024 and included 188 adult pythons and 168 juveniles.Rather than relying on occasional sightings, the team used radio telemetry to record the locations and habitat choices of individual snakes. The resulting dataset contained more than 4,000 observations, allowing the scientists to examine how often the reptiles entered trees and shrubs and whether certain conditions made this behaviour more likely.USGS reported that fewer than 3% of the recorded observations involved snakes positioned in trees or shrubs. Across the tracked animals, around 14% of adults and 17% of juveniles were documented using vegetation above the ground at least once.Why Burmese pythons climb trees in winterBoth young and mature snakes were more likely to enter trees during the cooler, drier months, with December and January standing out in the tracking records. For adult pythons, many of the sightings during this period involved basking. As reptiles depend on external sources of heat to regulate their body temperature, finding a suitable position in the sun can help them warm up when surrounding conditions become cooler.One documented encounter in January 2022 illustrates how high an adult python can climb. A male was observed basking on a coastal plain willow branch approximately 2.5 metres above the ground in Big Cypress National Preserve.A USGS researcher recorded the animal while carrying radio-tracking equipment nearby. Other observations revealed even greater heights. In February 2022, an adult male was first located on a Brazilian peppertree around five metres above the ground.Finding pythons remains a major challenge for Florida managersThe new findings have practical implications because locating Burmese pythons in the Everglades is already difficult. Their ability to remain concealed in dense vegetation, combined with their behaviour and habitat choices, makes routine detection unreliable.Current estimates suggest that the probability of finding an individual python during a detection effort can fall below 5%. Knowing that some individuals use trees during particular months gives wildlife managers another behaviour to consider when planning monitoring and removal work.Could climbing pythons pose a risk to nesting birdsThe study also raises questions about the possible interaction between Burmese pythons and native wildlife. The Everglades supports several bird species that nest in trees and shrubs, creating opportunities for encounters with predators capable of reaching elevated branches.During the tracking investigation, scientists did not record pythons attacking or eating birds in trees. However, earlier research has documented the reptiles feeding on bird nests in the region, including those belonging to Great Egrets and White Ibises.What the findings mean for the future of python researchThe investigation, published with contributions from the USGS and its collaborators, adds detail to the understanding of an invasive species that has proved difficult to study in the wild. Its findings show that describing Burmese pythons simply as ground-dwelling or generalist predators does not capture every aspect of their behaviour.Their occasional use of trees appears to be influenced by seasonal conditions, with cooler weather providing a possible explanation for increased basking activity. The relatively small proportion of arboreal observations also makes clear that climbing should be treated as one part of their behaviour rather than a defining characteristic.

articles.title: London Underground drivers to stage new strikes in coming months
articles.summary: The union is in dispute with London Underground over working arrangements for drivers.
articles.body:
London Underground drivers are to stage a series of 24-hour strikes in a long-running dispute over working arrangements, the Rail, Maritime and Transport (RMT) union has announced.

A series of walkouts will begin on 26 November, with further strikes planned for 17 December, 19 December, 4 January, 6 January, 17 February, 23 February and 25 February.

The action will be taken in opposition to Transport for London (TfL) plans to introduce a four-day working week.

The union says drivers will face longer hours driving trains and work longer days, but TfL said the change would be voluntary and would mean drivers work fewer hours overall.

London Tube strikes: What you need to know

A series of strikes in the spring over the same issue caused significant disruption across the network, with some lines being entirely closed.

Despite further talks being held since, RMT has not accepted TfL's proposals.

General secretary Eddie Dempsey said: "London Underground is attempting to dress up a wholesale attack on drivers' working conditions as a voluntary four-day week.

"Our members are being asked to spend more time driving trains, accept longer and more unpredictable shifts and surrender agreements that have been negotiated and defended over many years."

The union also said it believed the changes would "pave the way for hundreds of job cuts".

TfL said that drivers choosing to remain on a five-day week would be given a guarantee of remaining at the same depot.

Nick Dent, director of customer operations for London Underground, said: "This will give our colleagues a real, meaningful choice on their working pattern without having to change where they work.

"This will also mean less time at work for Tube drivers, while delivering a more efficient, reliable Tube service for our customers."

About half of the drivers on the network are members of the RMT union.

Many others are represented by the Aslef union, which said it was "surprised" by the action.

Finn Brennan, Aslef's full-time organiser on London Underground, said: "The voluntary four-day week gives Tube train drivers an extra 35 days off every year with rosters based on a 34-hour week in return for some changes to working conditions and moving to electronic, rather than paper-based, systems for booking on for duty.

"Management have agreed that anyone who wants to keep working a five-day week will be able to do so without suffering any detriment, and we will be holding them to that.

"A strike designed to stop people having the choice of a shorter working week and more time off is a strange choice to make."

Under the proposals, most drivers would see their working week reduced from 36 hours to 35 hours, according to TfL. Their contractual hours would remain the same because paid meal breaks would be introduced.

This effectively means drivers would work longer days, but fewer days each week and fewer overall hours each week.

The RMT instead wants a 32-hour week over four days, meaning drivers would work three fewer hours each week for the same salary.

The business group BusinessLDN said the strikes were likely to affect the hospitality sector in particular in the run-up to Christmas.

"These strikes will not bring any festive cheer to Londoners and visitors who rely on the Tube to get around the city," transport programme director Ed Richardson said.

"We urge both sides to reach an agreement urgently and avoid these damaging strikes."

articles.title: American start-up plans to sell sunlight at night with help from India’s Skyroot Aerospace; a scientific study warns the glow could affect the night sky up to 30 kilometres from the target
articles.summary: Sunlight at night, sold on demand by an American space start-up using Indian rockets, is moving from science fiction towards commercial reality.
articles.body: Sunlight at night, sold on demand by an American space start-up using Indian rockets, is moving from science fiction towards commercial reality. California-based Reflect Orbital plans to place giant mirrors in low-Earth orbit and steer reflected sunlight onto chosen spots on the ground after dark. Customers could include solar farms wanting longer generating hours, rescue teams searching disaster zones, and industrial sites working through the night. The company has booked two launches with Hyderabad-based Skyroot Aerospace, tying India directly to a service no business has sold before. The first launch will use Skyroot’s Vikram-1 rocket, the second its newer Vikram-1U.Sunlight you can dim or switch off; five-kilometre swathe, with defence sites and events in mindAccording to PTI, the company intends to build a constellation of satellites rather than a single mirror. The Vikram-1U, which will fly the second mission, has additional first-stage boosters and improved performance, the company’s statement added.The company says its sunlight can be switched off at any moment, with brightness adjustable across a five-kilometre swathe. Beyond energy and emergency work, it pitches the service to defence operations that need critical infrastructure lit up, and to organisers of events in public spaces who want memorable experiences.In 1993, Russian scientists and engineers sent a 65-foot mirror into orbit and used it to send a roving beam of sunlight down to Earth. The experiment, named Znamya, was successful, yet it was shelved for want of funds.The United States regulator licensed the demonstration satellite but not the light it would reflectAs The Conversation reported, the Federal Communications Commission authorised Reflect Orbital in July to deploy and operate Eärendil-1, its first orbital demonstrator. The licence, however, covers only radio communications, namely the frequencies used to send telemetry from, and commands to, the satellite. Astronomers asked the commission to impose safeguards against optical effects, but it declined, concluding that astronomy sits outside the scope of its rules. The American Astronomical Society and other groups have since challenged that decision.PTI reported that several environmental organisations have also urged the commission to scrap the permission. They argue that bright beams at night could disturb wildlife, interfere with astronomy studies and affect human circadian rhythms, the body’s sleep-and-wake cycle.What the scientific model says space-mirror glow would do to the night sky, far beyond the beamIt is tempting to imagine a mirror lighting only a single chosen site, but Earth’s atmosphere has no sharp edges. A peer-reviewed study in The Astrophysical Journal Letters modelled what happens as reflected sunlight passes through the air. Molecules and tiny airborne particles scatter part of the beam across the surrounding sky, and light that reaches the ground is reflected upwards and scattered again.For a proposed future mirror 54 metres wide, the study’s authors found the resulting sky glow could stay substantial far beyond the target area. At 14 kilometres from the beam, it could outshine a full Moon across most of the sky, and at 34 kilometres the sky towards the beam could still be brighter than under a full Moon. These are model predictions, not measurements from real space mirrors.The harms the authors describe begin inside the beam. Within the lit patch, which has a radius of about 2.5 kilometres, the ground would be lit to roughly 9.5 lux, about street-light level, and the mirror itself would shine about 40 times brighter than the full Moon. The sky would be as bright as dusk shortly after sunset, too bright for even the brightest stars to show, and the authors conclude that the night sky is lost within the illuminated patch. Outside the beam, they call the night sky seriously compromised up to about 30 kilometres, the distance reached over snow-covered ground. They say the pollution would far exceed the upward glow of a town of similar size, since street lighting covers only a small share of a town’s area. Their figures assume a cloudless atmosphere, and they warn that thin high cloud lit by the beam could make the pollution visible from much larger distances.Eärendil-1 would be one-ninth as bright as that 54-metre mirror, the paper notes, which still means about four times full-Moon illumination over the same patch. The authors calculate that 400 such mirrors lighting one patch at once would reach about 10,000 times full-Moon brightness, with a glow visible from 80 kilometres, and they note that Reflect Orbital’s wider plan is a constellation of about 50,000 of the larger mirrors. The Astrophysical Journal Letters paper also says the commission approved the demonstrator without considering environmental and safety impacts, and that Reflect Orbital’s plans neither quantify the light pollution nor consider the environmental damage it could cause.A Reflect Orbital spokesperson told The Conversation that most people and places will never see the light. Customers, the spokesperson said, would need permits, local authority sign-off and identity checks, and anyone who does not want the light would not receive it.Launching from India could force a space regulator to rule on deliberately reflected sunlightA launch from India requires authorisation from the Indian National Space Promotion and Authorisation Centre. Its rules cover launch safety, registration and environmental effects, and they specifically require operators to limit negative effects on Earth or in space, including adverse changes to the atmosphere. No publicly available authorisation had shown how the centre would treat deliberately reflected light at the time of the analysis.Jurisdiction is also unclear. Reflect Orbital is American, Skyroot and the launch site are Indian, and the spacecraft could illuminate territory in a third country, while atmospheric scattering could carry the effects beyond the intended target. That leaves open whether a country must agree before a foreign operator lights up a site within its borders, how a neighbouring community or observatory hit by scattered light would be heard, and which regulator could make a space mirror operator change its behaviour.Eärendil-1 could give regulators real brightness data before sunlight becomes a paid serviceEärendil-1 will carry an 18-by-18-metre reflector, and its flight could give regulators measurements of brightness, atmospheric scattering and how accurately reflected light can be controlled. Reflect Orbital’s co-founder and chief executive, Ben Nowack, said in the company statement that, having been licensed in July, Reflect Orbital will keep working with astronomers, local communities and regulators to earn the right to scale up. Questions over who may switch the light on, and who may object when some of it lands beyond the customer’s boundary, become much harder once reflected sunlight is a commercial service rather than an experiment.

articles.title: How octopuses squeeze through holes that seem impossibly tiny
articles.summary: Octopuses are famous for slipping through seemingly impossible gaps. In a new study, scientists mapped how they do it, describing two distinct strategies.
articles.body: Octopuses are famous for slipping through seemingly impossible gaps. Scientists have now mapped how they do it, finding that these marine invertebrates organize their eight arms and soft bodies into a sequence that changes when the opening gets tighter — a strategy that could offer lessons for robots designed to enter confined spaces. Unlike humans and other animals with rigid skeletons, octopuses have extremely flexible bodies built around what scientists call a muscular hydrostat, a system of muscles that provides both support and movement without bones. Their eight dexterous arms can bend and elongate, while their central mantle can change shape. The animal's circulatory system is also suited to contortions: major blood vessels have muscular pumping systems that help keep blood moving locally even when part of the body is constricted. "In nature, octopuses have the ability to move through spaces smaller than their bodies, a capability called squeezing behavior," said Wenci Xin, a researcher at the National University of Singapore's Soft Robotics Lab and one of the authors of the study, published in the Journal of Experimental Biology. "We explored whether there is a general pattern in how these animals perform this behavior that could be applied to robots in the future." The researchers made videos of three sub-adult common octopuses squeezing through an adjustable opening. They discerned two main strategies: a three-step process employed by the octopuses when the opening was wider than the distance between the animal's eyes, and a four-step process used when it was narrower. "At the beginning, we expected the animals to use the same strategy. ... We were surprised when we found that the strategy changed," Xin said. In the three-step maneuver, an octopus first probed the opening with one arm, moved several more arms through, then used the inserted arms against the partition to pull the remaining arms, head and mantle through. With a tighter opening, the octopus added a step, pulling the remaining arms through before squeezing its head and mantle through separately. It is not clear what determines the narrowest gap an octopus can squeeze through. The animal's beak, which functions as its jaws and is its only rigid body part, has long been considered the limiting factor, but Xin said the experiments suggest it may instead be the size of the arms near the body. For an octopus, squeezing into tight spaces can provide an escape route and access to prey that other marine creatures cannot easily reach. "The idea is that the octopuses use the tactile sense on the arms to investigate the opening," said Michael Kuba, a biologist at the University of Naples Federico II and co-author of the study. Different octopus species may not tackle tight spaces in the same way. The common octopus is a generalist predator in coastal waters, particularly around rocky shores, where there are many holes to squeeze through, Kuba said. Species living on sandy seabeds or those with very different body shapes and arm lengths might use different strategies to negotiate openings, Kuba added. The researchers hope that understanding how octopuses solve this problem could help engineers design more versatile robots for navigating similarly confined spaces. Search-and-rescue robots designed to move through debris are often long and slender because they need a small cross-section to navigate narrow gaps, Xin said. An octopus-inspired robot potentially could carry more equipment, with flexible arms equipped with different sensors, tools or communication devices, Xin added. Building one presents an engineering challenge: its arms would need to be soft enough to squeeze through narrow openings, but strong and dexterous enough to bend, twist and stretch while pulling the rest of the body through, Xin said. Conventional actuators needed to control such complex movements typically add rigid components, making the robot stiffer. For Kuba, the study also highlights how much remains to be learned about the animals themselves. "Humans feel attracted to octopuses as the soft intelligence in the ocean," Kuba said. "But we know very little about how the octopus lives its daily life."

articles.title: Pentagon offers battery startup 6K $250M loan to build US factory | TechCrunch
articles.summary: The Pentagon has conditionally approved a $250 million loan to help 6K scale up its microwave-plasma battery material manufacturing process.
articles.body:
Batteries are everywhere, even on the battlefield, which helps explain the Pentagon’s recent interest in building more domestic manufacturing capacity.

The 12-year-old, North Andover, Massachusetts-based startup 6K announced Thursday that it won conditional approval for a $250 million loan from the Department of Defense to build a factory in Tennessee. The plant will use a unique microwave-powered process to produce battery materials that don’t rely on Chinese suppliers.

The company previously received a $50 million grant from the Department of Energy under the Bipartisan Infrastructure Law, though that 2023 grant was canceled by the Trump administration in a chaotic sweep of Biden-era awards, forcing 6K to reapply.

The factory was originally slated to open in 2024, but the grant cancelation and uncertainties in the EV market forced the company to rejigger its plans .

6K’s manufacturing process uses microwaves to heat metals into a plasma and then deposit them onto a surface, reducing the number of steps required to make cathode material, a key battery component. The company says the process can work on a number of different battery types, including lithium iron phosphate (LFP).

articles.title: T-Mobile chairman says 'welcome to the party' to Elon Musk and Starlink Mobile — but says SpaceX will need $200 billion to become a serious mobile rival
articles.summary: Starlink Mobile will need to invest a minimum of $200 billion in spectrum, towers, and antennas according to a major telecoms exec.
articles.body:
When you buy through links on our articles, Future and its syndication partners may earn a commission.

The chairman of T-Mobile and CEO of its parent company has commented on Starlink Mobile

He argues that a $200 billion investment in spectrum and infrastructure is needed for it to compete

Despite that, he's taking it seriously and sees parallels with Tesla and the car industry

Between partnering with Qualcomm and getting the green light to operate internationally , SpaceX has taken some major steps towards making Starlink Mobile a rival to the big carriers. And that's just been acknowledged by Tim Höttges — the chairman of T-Mobile and CEO of its parent company, Deutsche Telekom — in a recent earnings call where he said that "I take his [Elon Musk] attempt serious [sic]."

In the Deutsche Telekom conference call , Höttges went on to highlight just how much work — and investment — will be required for this attempt to actually deliver a real rival.

Firstly, Starlink Mobile will likely require a lot more spectrum than it currently has, with Höttges saying "he [Musk] has now bought 76 megahertz of spectrum. By the way, we have 400 megahertz. So if you now say, okay, he can buy the spectrum prospectively, do your math. These are kind of triple digit billions, which are needed to gain the spectrum position."

And it's not just spectrum — Starlink Mobile will also need a lot of infrastructure on the ground, with Höttges explaining that "then he has to build a network. I can tell you, we have 85,000 towers. No, he can rent towers, no question. But this is another $20 billion to $30 billion, which are required. Put antennas on it. Okay, you can buy antennas and you can get maybe even in a cheaper way or you construct it in a new way, but you need money for that."

Between all that, Höttges concludes that Starlink Mobile will need "at least minimum $200 billion" to "play" in this industry, and likely more. And even then, it's an industry which Höttges argues T-Mobile and the other major carriers have "professionalized over the last twenty years" — suggesting that even with that investment, Starlink Mobile will lack the experience of the other carriers.

Still, it doesn't sound like Höttges is totally counting Musk's telecom dreams out, remarking at the end of all that "welcome to the party." So this looks set to be a long and expensive road for SpaceX and Starlink Mobile — and experts mostly agree that becoming the fourth big mobile network in the US will be a major challenge...

articles.title: Meet Aaryan Ghorpade, the North Carolina student who built a prototype for a free roadkill-mapping platform and has now won a first-place award for his plan to make American roads safer for wildlife
articles.summary: North Carolina student Aaryan Ghorpade has won a national competition after creating a free online mapping tool designed to reduce wildlife deaths on
articles.body: North Carolina student Aaryan Ghorpade has won a national competition after creating a free online mapping tool designed to reduce wildlife deaths on American roads. Ghorpade took first place in the 16 to 18 age group of the 2024 "A Voice for Animals" contest with his project, "EcoRoute: Mitigating Wildlife-Vehicle Collisions." The annual competition is jointly organised by the Animal Welfare Institute and Humane Education Network. It recognises young people who use creative ideas and community involvement to solve problems affecting animal welfare. As reported by the Animal Welfare Institute, Ghorpade developed a working early version of a free online roadkill mapping platform. The tool collects information to identify roads where vehicle collisions with wildlife happen frequently. This information can help transport departments and local authorities decide where safety improvements are most needed.Technology targeting high-collision zonesWildlife and vehicle collisions cause more than one million animal deaths every day in the United States. They also lead to major property damage and injuries to people. State agencies often find it difficult to identify dangerous road areas because reports are collected through different systems. Ghorpade created EcoRoute as a free platform that anyone can access. It brings together reports of wildlife collisions and uses the information to create heat maps showing high-risk areas. By identifying the exact places where animals regularly try to cross roads, the software helps planners decide where safety measures could be most useful. These measures include special fencing to guide animals, underpasses that allow wildlife to cross beneath roads, and lower speed limits. According to information published by the Humane Education Network, Ghorpade's project also includes a practical plan for improving transport policies. His proposal looked at how state transport departments could use free, publicly available data in their long-term road planning without spending large amounts on monitoring.National recognition for student innovationThe "A Voice for Animals" contest was created to encourage young people to get involved in protecting animals. It offers cash prizes to students who present carefully researched ideas for solving animal welfare problems. The Animal Welfare Institute announced that Ghorpade received the $600 first-place prize in the 16 to 18 age category. Judges assessed entries based on original ideas, practical use, and their possible impact on protecting animals. "The innovative ideas presented by these students demonstrate a deep commitment to compassion and problem solving," stated representatives from the Animal Welfare Institute in their official contest announcement. "Aaryan Ghorpade's work highlights how technology can serve as a vital tool in creating safer environments for native wildlife." The 2024 competition also recognised students from around the world who worked on different animal protection issues. Their projects covered topics such as birds hitting windows and the protection of marine habitats.Practical application for transportation planningRoad projects designed to protect wildlife, including animal overpasses and underpasses, can greatly reduce road deaths when they are built in areas where many animals cross. However, local planners need reliable information about these locations to support spending money on such projects. Ghorpade's early version of EcoRoute offers an affordable option for local governments that want to use data when planning road improvements. Because the mapping platform is free to access, members of the public and volunteers working in the field can report wildlife sightings. These reports help create updated data that environmental agencies can use. Following his competition win, Ghorpade plans to continue improving EcoRoute. His next steps include making changes to the software's data collection and processing systems and working with regional wildlife protection groups to test the platform on roads across North Carolina.

articles.title: Twenty black grouse were moved from the North Pennines to the North York Moors in 2024; the next breeding season produced 12 chicks, likely the area's first successful breeding in nearly 200 years
articles.summary: Wildlife conservation is tricky.
articles.body: Wildlife conservation is tricky. The goal is never just to sustain the animal's population but also to make the habitat and surrounding conditions suitable for them to reproduce and establish a population. The black grouse, a fairly rare bird in the United Kingdom, has brought encouraging news as part of a conservation effort. But can you imagine the possible return of a species to an area where it once thrived? After nearly two centuries without any reliable records of successful breeding in the North York Moors, the birds have now successfully fledged 12 chicks in the area, offering hope for their return.According to a report published by the Game and Wildlife Conservation Trust (GWCT) on September 22, 2025, 20 black grouse were moved from their stronghold in the North Pennines to the North York Moors during the autumn of 2024. The translocation was part of the Black Grouse Range Expansion Project, an initiative that was led by the GWCT with the aim of expanding the range of one of Britain's rarest birds.Researchers caught the birds, including 10 males and 10 females, at their night-time roosting sites and took them to the release location, where they fitted 16 of the 20 translocated birds, comprising 8 males and 8 females, with radio tags to monitor their movements and survival. But by spring, 7 males and 7 females remained in the area.The results from the first breeding season were particularly encouraging. Of the seven males that remained in the area by spring, all established what are known as leks. These are traditional display grounds where male black grouse gather and perform elaborate displays to attract females and compete for mating opportunities. The birds use these gatherings as part of their breeding behaviour, making them an important part of the species' reproductive cycle.The females also started nesting in surrounding areas. All 7 females that remained in the area by spring attempted to breed; 5 nests successfully hatched chicks, while two were abandoned. 4 of the 5 females whose nests hatched went on to raise broods of one, two, four and five chicks, respectively. Together, these accounted for 12 chicks that successfully fledged. Although individual females had occasionally been spotted in the area in recent years, the latest findings are likely to mark the first successful breeding there in nearly 200 years.Why the birds need suitable habitats to surviveHowever, moving the birds was only one part of the conservation effort. For a species to establish itself in a new landscape, the availability of suitable habitat is equally important. Black grouse depend on a combination of moorland and surrounding farmland habitats, where they can find food, shelter and suitable places to nest.The North York Moors was selected as a potential location following several years of habitat improvements along the fringes of moorland managed for grouse shooting. These included removing conifer woodland and restoring the land to bog, heath and scrub woodland. Moorland grasslands have also been managed to control bracken and encourage the recovery of plants such as bilberry and heather.The project has also involved cooperation between land managers and gamekeepers across different estates. According to the GWCT, targeted predator management, alongside vegetation management, has been important in creating conditions where the birds can breed successfully. Such work needs to take place across a wider landscape rather than being restricted to the immediate release site.A rare bird that needs conservation attentionBlack grouse are classified as a Red List species in the United Kingdom due to the decline in their breeding population. They were once found across every county in England, but their present-day range is largely restricted to the North Pennines, which covers parts of County Durham, Northumberland, Cumbria and North Yorkshire.The GWCT reports that the number of displaying males in the North Pennines has remained broadly stable, fluctuating between 1,000 and 2,000 over the past 25 years. However, the fact that 96 per cent of the remaining black grouse are found along the edges of moorland managed for red grouse highlights how restricted their distribution has become. Another challenge has been the geographical separation between existing populations and the North York Moors. The two areas are divided by approximately 30 kilometres of lowland farmland in the Vale of Mowbray, which does not provide suitable habitat for the birds to move through naturally.What happens next?A conservation milestone has now been achieved following a reintroduction project that began in 2024. In a report published on June 19, 2026, the GWCT announced that the number of displaying male black grouse recorded across 18 monitored estates had increased from 557 in 2025 to 894 in spring 2026. However, these figures relate to the GWCT's wider monitoring programme across northern England, not exclusively to the reintroduced population in the North York Moors. This shows a 61% increase in just a year.But the conservation effort, having seen this wonderful success, is now entering its third consecutive year of translocations, according to a report published by Shooting UK in September 2026, which says that another transfer of black grouse to the North York Moors is planned for the autumn.

articles.title: For more than 60 years, visitors walked through a cave in Spain without noticing hundreds of Ice Age engravings; archaeologists have now identified 280 motifs, making it one of Mediterranean Iberia's largest art sites
articles.summary: Not all art is exhibited or put on display.
articles.body: Not all art is exhibited or put on display. Some of it remains hidden in plain sight, etched into rock and can go unnoticed for centuries, even when people have been walking past them for decades. In a cave in Spain, hundreds of such engravings has now opened up new avenues of research, offering archaeologists a fresh understanding of the prehistoric artistic traditions of the Iberian Peninsula.A research conducted by Josep Maria Vergès Bosch and Míriam Salas-Altès of the Catalan Institute of Human Paleoecology and Social Evolution (IPHES-CERCA), was published in Antiquity on 5 November 2026. This report notes the cave to now be the 3rd largest known Palaeolithic cave art assemblage along the Mediterranean side of the Iberian Peninsula.The discovery has brought close attention to the Cova de la Font Major in Catalonia, northeastern Spain, where archaeologists have identified 280 Palaeolithic motifs, including motifs of animals and several non-figurative designs. Interestingly, people were aware of this cave before, and it was open to visitors as well. People have been visiting Cova de la Font Major since at least the 12th century, while its entrance became widely frequented by visitors, speleologists and treasure hunters from 1957 onwards.Despite the number of people who had entered the cave over the years, its prehistoric engravings had not come to light. According to research in Antiquity, the discovery was made on 30 October 2019, during an archaeological visit to a section known as the Gatoneres de Cal Palletes. One of the researchers noticed that some marks on the walls appeared different from the more recent inscriptions and graffiti that spread across the surrounding surface.When examined closely, it was deduced that these markings belonged to the Palaeolithic period, opening up to us a whole new world of meaning and art that predates us.The researchers had not expected to find a plethora of such artworks here, given that the cave been previously considered an unlikely space for palaeolithic engravings, given the uneven surface of the rocks. However, the discovery has now confirmed that certain sections of the walls, particularly their marl layers, had provided suitable surfaces for engraving.But the cave doesn't go on to reveal the world of the prehistoric people to us, but also the markings made by visitors in the last few decades. As alongside the geometric markings, the parallel lines, and representation of animals including a bear, are names and dates of the visitors on the wall, where these artistic traditions were liely missed.What do the engravings reveal?The artistic engravings were reportedly, produced through incisions made into the rock, with scraping also used in some instances. The marks are not all alike, and their different forms provide researchers with material to examine the ways prehistoric communities expressed themselves through images and symbols.The collection identified so far comprises 280 motifs, of which 55 are zoomorphic representations, meaning figures depicting animals. The remaining motifs include non-figurative engravings, such as lines and geometric forms, which do not necessarily represent recognisable living beings.An important aspect of the discovery is that the collection is not limited to a handful of isolated animal figures. The researchers point out that around 75% of known Palaeolithic art assemblages along the Iberian Mediterranean coast contain no more than five animal figures, while more than 90% have no more than 20. With 55 zoomorphic representations, Cova de la Font Major therefore stands out in comparison with many other known sites.Reconsidering prehistoric art in northeastern SpainBeyond the number of engravings, this discovery also challenges an established understanding that Palaeolithic art was concentrated in the Iberian Peninsula. The Iberian Peninsula, which comprises present-day Spain and Portugal, contains more than 50% of all documented Upper Palaeolithic cave art in Europe. Its distribution, however, is far from even.A large concentration has traditionally been found in the Franco-Cantabrian region, an area spanning parts of modern-day France and northern Spain. But, North-eastern Iberia, particularly Catalonia, was considered relatively poor in Palaeolithic cave art. So much so that before this discovery, only 2 representations had been identified across the region.However, this newly documented engraving suggests that this apparent absence may not have reflected the actual artistic practices of the people who lived there. Moreover, the sheer quantity of engravings now discovered suggests that it may have supported much more substantial human activity than previously understood. Instead, the researchers also found that the motifs at Cova de la Font Major differ from those associated with the neighbouring Franco-Cantabrian tradition, suggesting that northeastern Iberia could have its own distinct artistic traditions.Archaeologists have not merely discovered ancient drawings but have recovered evidence of a previously under-recognised prehistoric artistic tradition, transforming how researchers now understand the cultural landscape of Ice Age Europe. This finding informs not only about the art produced but also raises questions about how densely populated this region may have been during the Paleolithic era. A previously marginal area in discussions of artistic activity has revealed a whole new artistic history to the world.

articles.title: UN climate talks start in a year of disasters, energy price shocks and fast rising temperatures
articles.summary: The 31st Conference of Parties, or COP31, starts Monday, though the U.S. is not expected to attend. Thus far, the world has failed to meet its goals to curb global warming.
articles.body: Three stories about climate change are playing out like popular movie genres as United Nations climate negotiations begin in Antalya, Turkey. There's the horror story. Many scientists believe global warming is accelerating. Two months ago, the U.N. readjusted its decade-old goal of limiting global temperature rise to 1.5 degrees Celsius (2.7 degrees Fahrenheit) because the world is blowing past that threshold. The fallout from rising temperatures is felt globally, with Europe's deadly summer heat waves and Nepal's devastating flooding as stark examples. There's the love triangle. For more than a century, the world has been powered by coal, oil and gas. This love affair spurred economic development, as well as the emissions warming the planet. But renewable energy is capturing some of the world's attention because it's cheaper and cleaner than fossil fuels. Instead of switching from one to the other, the world is using both to meet demand from power-hungry artificial intelligence and ever-growing economic development. This isn't helping curb climate change. Then there's the war movie. Russia's 2022 invasion of Ukraine triggered a European energy shock. This year the United States and Israel bombed Iran. The conflict closed the Strait of Hormuz and sent fossil fuel prices skyrocketing, forcing nations to rethink their energy systems. These stories are colliding as the 31st Conference of Parties, or COP31, starts Monday with speeches from world leaders and will later dig into how to follow through on past climate pledges. A key issue this year is the implementation of promises to transition away from fossil fuels. Co-host Turkey is also pushing a separate plan that would help do that by shifting more global energy use — including transportation — to electricity generated from solar and wind power. Negotiators also will hash out how to provide promised funds to poor countries to switch to renewables, adapt to a warmer world and recover from climate-induced damage. “It’s really the moment that we place a magnifying lens on what’s happening in the world on climate change, both good and bad,” David Waskow, international climate chief at the World Resources Institute, said. While the U.S. is the world’s largest historic carbon polluter, it skipped last year's COP and isn't expected to participate this year. “There’s always two topics in the climate negotiations that are relevant and difficult,” said Niklas Höhne, co-founder of Germany’s NewClimate Institute. “The first one is who produces emissions (and) how much. That is difficult enough. But what is even more complicated is the other issue, and that is who pays. And on this one, we are particularly in a difficult situation because the U.S., as the largest contributor, has dropped out. And there’s no other player who can jump in.” Global climate efforts are off track Eleven years ago, the world was on track to hit 4 C (7.2 F) of warming above preindustrial levels by the end of the century. In 2015, nations set the goal of keeping warming to below 2 C (3.6 F), but with a preferred limit of 1.5 C (2.7 F), as measured over a multi-year period. Now, the world is at 1.4 C (2.5 F) of warming and is hurtling toward 2.6 C (4.7 F), the U.N. found. October 2026 was the hottest October on record, and 2026 is virtually certain to end up as the second year to exceed the 1.5 degree Celsius level, behind 2024, the European climate agency Copernicus announced Friday. “We have failed so far,” said Johan Rockström, director of Germany’s Potsdam Institute for Climate Impact Research. Rockström said Earth will likely experience more extreme weather, such as floods, droughts and storms, and may soon reach “tipping points,” such as ocean currents changing and the Amazon rainforest collapsing. It comes down to fossil fuels Even though burning fossil fuels is the main cause of warming, it has rarely been targeted in final documents agreed upon at the conference, mostly because those decisions require consensus. “The reason we are seeing the breach of 1.5 degrees Celsius of warming is because we avoided the absolutely fundamental question of how climate change happened and what’s responsible, the source of the problem and that’s fossil fuels,” said Harjeet Singh, founding director of Satat Sampada Climate Foundation. “Unless and until we resolve the issue of fossil fuel phase out, we will not be able to deal with the problem.” Brazil, which hosted COP30 last year, this month released a detailed voluntary roadmap for how countries could transition away from fossil fuels. The roadmap is meant to turn the “big problem” of reducing fossil fuels into “smaller actionable solutions,” Ana Toni, who served as CEO of last year's climate talks, said. One key thing nations must do is stop subsidizing fossil fuels, she said. The U.N. estimates fossil fuel subsidies globally hit $1.1 trillion this year. “What’s standing in the way is not so much technology as governments and incumbent industries,” said Bill Hare, CEO of Climate Analytics. “One cannot underestimate the power and influence of the fossil fuel industry in slowing down action.” Climate talks bring hope and frustration Barbados youth activist Ashley Lashley's first COP was five years ago. She was frustrated by the lack of progress then, but hopeful because there was urgency to keep the 1.5-degree goal alive. Lashley still attends negotiations with some hope, but she is more frustrated than ever. She said “the science has become more alarming, but yet politically we seem to be negotiating how much failure we are prepared to tolerate.” Qiyun Woo, a Singaporean youth environmentalist, said her generation is tired of “seeing their present and futures blanketed in wildfire smoke, in devastating floods (and) landslides." What gives most experts hope is how cheap solar and wind energy are, along with electric car growth, strengthening the economic argument for transitioning away from fossil fuels. “It has never been as easy to reduce emissions as it is today because, again, this year, renewable energy has been developing faster than before,” Höhne said. Hope for progress on the sidelines Much of the work at climate negotiations happens on the sidelines, where not everyone has to agree and some nations do more than others. One important sideline initiative this year is Turkey's goal of increasing electricity's share of global energy use from 21% to 35% by 2035, preferably by using renewable power. Mohamed Adow, a veteran COP observer and director of Power Shift Africa, said the conference is taking place at a time when the world is deeply fragmented. “The closure of the Strait of Hormuz has intensified economic and energy security pressures," he said. "We don’t expect this particular conference to be able to sufficiently respond to the present day challenge ... that is affecting livelihoods and economies.” The climate talks are hindered by the continued absence of the U.S., Adow said, adding that it wasn't fair to nations like Nepal, which have to face catastrophic destruction alone while the world's wealthiest country and biggest polluter sits on the fence. “A time will come when we will have to hold the U.S. accountable for the climate harms that it’s caused,” he said.

articles.title: Scientists tested the six-tonne Altar Stone at Stonehenge after earlier research pointed to north-east Scotland, but a new November 5 study found no matching rock source there, leaving its ancient journey unresolved
articles.summary: It is surprising how the stonehenge, one of the most recognisable and famous prehistoric monuments, still holds its secrets.
articles.body: It is surprising how the stonehenge, one of the most recognisable and famous prehistoric monuments, still holds its secrets. One such secret it is hiding is of a six-tonne rock, ironically.For more than a century, scientists have been trying to work out where one particular stone at Stonehenge came from. The Altar Stone, which lies partly buried at the centre of the monument, has had geologists looking across Britain for answers. A discovery in 2024 published in Natureseemed to have finally solved the mystery, pointing towards northeast Scotland. However, a new study published published in the Journal of the Geological Society on November 5, 2026, has complicated things again. Researchers have found no matching rock source in the Scottish locations they investigated, leaving the stone's origins uncertain.The mystery of StonehengeSituated on Salisbury Plain in Wiltshire, England, the Stonehenge has stood for thousands of years, attracting archaeologists, historians and curious visitors alike. Its construction began around 3000 BC, with several additions and changes made over the next two millennia.But building a monument of this scale was no small feat. Its enormous stones had to be sourced, transported and arranged long before modern machinery existed. And they did not all come from the same place. Some of the smaller stones, known as bluestones, travelled approximately 225 kilometres from the Preseli Hills in west Wales to reach the site.Among the many stones that make up the monument, the Altar Stone stands out from the other towering sarsen stones that dominate Stonehenge. It is a large slab of Old Red Sandstone, measuring approximately 4.9 metres long and weighing around six tonnes. Unlike the other stones that stand upright, it lies flat beneath the collapsed remains of the Great Trilithon, partly hidden by the grass.Where it was quarried is a question scientists have struggled to answer for years.From Wales to ScotlandFor nearly 100 years, the prevailing theory was that the Altar Stone had come from west Wales. This seemed like a reasonable explanation, considering that several of Stonehenge's other stones had travelled from the region. However, scientists began questioning this assumption as they learnt more about the stone's geological composition.In August 2024, a study published in Nature offered a rather surprising possibility. Researchers examined tiny mineral grains trapped inside fragments of the Altar Stone, including zircon, apatite and rutile. These minerals carry chemical and age signatures that can help scientists trace the geological history of a rock.Think of them as a geological fingerprint. By studying the minerals and comparing their characteristics with rocks from different regions, researchers can narrow down where a particular stone may have originated.The results pointed towards the Orcadian Basin in northeast Scotland. The mineral signatures closely matched those found in the region's Old Red Sandstone, suggesting that the Altar Stone had travelled from much farther north than previously imagined.If the theory was correct, the stone had covered a journey of more than 700 kilometres to reach Salisbury Plain. How Neolithic communities managed to move something so heavy across such a distance was another question altogether. Whether it travelled by land, sea or a combination of both, the discovery offered a glimpse into just how connected prehistoric communities might have been.The search begins againThe Scottish theory was exciting, but scientists needed more than a close mineral match to identify the exact source. Several geological locations can share similar mineral ages, even if their overall composition is different. This meant researchers had to look beyond the minerals that first pointed towards Scotland.In the latest study, an international team led by geologist Duncan Pirrie examined the Altar Stone in much greater detail. Published in the Journal of the Geological Society, the research brought together different techniques to study its structure, mineral composition, chemistry and isotopic characteristics.The team examined eight fragments held in museum collections that could be confidently linked to the Altar Stone. They also carried out non-invasive measurements on small exposed areas of the monument itself. Researchers then compared these findings with geological samples collected from potential source locations in northeast Scotland. Around 70 samples were collected from Scottish rock outcrops and taken back for laboratory testing.This time, the scientists were looking for a much more complete match. Along with mineral ages, they examined features such as chrome spinel, clay minerals and barium chemistry. These additional characteristics helped build a more detailed picture of what the original rock should look like.And the results were not quite what they expected. None of the Scottish locations examined had the complete combination of geological characteristics found in the Altar Stone. Although the mineral ages still pointed towards an ancient source associated with Laurentia, a geological landmass that once existed in the Northern Hemisphere, the evidence was not enough to identify the Orcadian Basin as its precise origin.So, where did the stone come from?The latest findings do not mean that scientists have returned to square one. They have, in fact, managed to narrow down the possibilities. The research makes a northeast Scottish origin very unlikely, while also providing a more detailed geological fingerprint that can be used to investigate other locations.Southern Britain has also been ruled out as the source. Other parts of Scotland, northern England and even Ireland remain possible locations for further investigation.The distinction matters because finding where the stone came from could tell us much more than its geological history. It could reveal how far Neolithic communities travelled, how they exchanged resources and how they organised the movement of enormous objects across landscapes. It could also help researchers understand the connections that existed between communities thousands of years ago, long before written records could tell us about them.For now, the Altar Stone remains firmly in place, with its origins somewhere beyond the boundaries of what scientists have managed to establish. Every new study brings another piece of the puzzle, even when it eliminates an answer that once seemed convincing. Perhaps the next geological expedition will finally uncover its birthplace. Until then, Stonehenge's six-tonne mystery is still waiting to be moved, at least on paper.

articles.title: Starlink Mobile: All the news on SpaceX’s major mobile carrier ambitions
articles.summary: SpaceX has plans to make Starlink Mobile a major mobile carrier in the US. Here are all the updates on SpaceX’s plan to merge its satellite network with 5G towers here on Earth.
articles.body: SpaceX has declared that it’s going to make Starlink Mobile a “major” mobile carrier. The Elon Musk-owned company has already deployed thousands of direct-to-cell satellites, but its next big challenge is building out its 5G network here on Earth. As part of its plans to rival AT&T, Verizon, and T-Mobile, SpaceX has inked a deal with Qualcomm, which will deploy its cellular technology across tens of thousands of 5G cell sites starting in 2027. SpaceX is also reportedly in talks to buy Boost Mobile, potentially allowing it to launch Starlink Mobile through the service. Another report suggests SpaceX may tap into 80,000 cell sites across the US to build out its network. SpaceX’s big plans have garnered some reactions in the telecom industry. Tim Höttges, the CEO of T-Mobile’s parent company Deutsche Telekom, said he takes SpaceX’s plans “super serious” but that it could cost Musk more than $200 billion to pull off. Follow along for the latest updates on Starlink’s major mobile carrier ambitions.

articles.title: Mercúrio contaminou mais sítios arqueológicos maias do que se pensava | G1
articles.standfirst: Análise de sedimentos de lagos no México encontrou níveis elevados de mercúrio por séculos; contaminação atingiu organismos aquáticos e pode ter exposto populações maias.
articles.summary: Análise de sedimentos de lagos no México encontrou níveis elevados de mercúrio por séculos; contaminação atingiu organismos aquáticos e pode ter exposto populações maias.
articles.body:
Turistas escalam pirâmide maia de Nohoch Mul no sítio arqueológico de Coba. — Foto: REUTERS/Victor Gerardo Ruiz Garcia

Para os antigos maias, o cinábrio — um mineral de cor vermelha vibrante — tinha um profundo significado sagrado, representando o sangue, a vida e a alma. Eles o utilizavam amplamente como pigmento em murais e templos, além de empregá-lo em cerimônias e ritos funerários. O que eles não sabiam é que o cinábrio é composto principalmente por mercúrio, que pode ser altamente tóxico.

Pesquisas anteriores mostraram como o mercúrio do cinábrio deixou contaminação duradoura nos locais de certas cidades maias antigas, como Tikal, na Guatemala. Um novo estudo revela que essa contaminação era mais generalizada do que se sabia anteriormente e documenta como o mercúrio, após se infiltrar no solo e nos corpos d’água ao redor, se mostrou mortal para muitos organismos aquáticos.

Os pesquisadores obtiveram amostras de núcleo do fundo de lagos em duas antigas cidades maias na península de Yucatán, no México — o sítio bem estudado de Coba e o pouco conhecido de Xcach.

As amostras mostraram um pico de mercúrio em Coba, com início por volta de 250 d.C. e duração de cerca de 150 anos, coincidindo com o início da era de ouro da civilização maia, conhecida como Período Clássico. Em Xcach, houve um pico por volta de 125 d.C. a 200 d.C., pouco antes do Período Clássico; em seguida, um segundo pico mais ou menos na mesma época que o de Coba; e um terceiro pico de aproximadamente 535 d.C. a 820 d.C., que se estendeu até cerca do fim do Período Clássico.

O estudo documenta a contaminação por mercúrio nas planícies do norte da região maia, uma área onde os registros sobre mercúrio eram até então escassos, e revela algumas das maiores concentrações de mercúrio já registradas na era maia.

Muitas das grandes cidades maias entraram em colapso e foram abandonadas no final do Período Clássico. Várias hipóteses foram apresentadas para explicar essa calamidade, incluindo mudanças climáticas e guerras. A nova pesquisa sugere o envenenamento por mercúrio como um fator adicional.

“Nosso estudo mostra que os limites estabelecidos pelas regulamentações modernas de toxicologia e poluição foram amplamente ultrapassados nos níveis mais tóxicos durante séculos nas proximidades de Coba e Xcach”, afirmou o paleolimnologista Matt Waters, professor de ciências ambientais da Universidade de Auburn, no Alabama, e autor principal do estudo publicado na revista Science Advances.

“Além disso, medimos vários marcadores biológicos nos sedimentos, como bactérias, algas, cianobactérias, organismos com concha e mosquitos, que diminuíram ou desapareceram nos lagos, o que significa que o mercúrio havia se infiltrado em vários níveis da cadeia alimentar”, disse Waters.

O mercúrio no corpo humano pode causar danos ao sistema nervoso central, ao cérebro, aos rins, aos pulmões e ao coração.

“Embora não demonstremos isso em nossos registros de sedimentos, esse movimento trófico sugere que o povo maia pode ter sido exposto ao mercúrio por meio do consumo de água ou peixes”, disse a coautora do estudo Savanna Wooten, pesquisadora de pós-doutorado no Jones Center, no centro de pesquisa Ichauway, na Geórgia.

“Essa pesquisa pouco contribui para vincular diretamente o mercúrio ao declínio das cidades maias da Era Clássica. Mas acrescenta mais um fator de estresse à crescente lista de pressões ambientais e climáticas documentadas como tendo ocorrido simultaneamente com os maias do Período Clássico”, acrescentou.

articles.title: In 2018, Elon Musk donated $480,350 for Flint school water filters and $423,000 to buy laptops for students; he also pledged that he would 'fund fixing the water in any house that has ...'
articles.summary: In 2018, the SpaceX CEO Elon Musk’s foundation donated about $480,000 to install water filtration systems in Flint, Michigan, schools, along with $423,000
articles.body: In 2018, the SpaceX CEO Elon Musk’s foundation donated about $480,000 to install water filtration systems in Flint, Michigan, schools, along with $423,000 for student laptops. The foundation funded 136 filtering stations that serve twelve school buildings. The donation came years after Flint’s water supply was contaminated with catastrophic levels of lead in 2014, when officials switched to a cheaper water source.Podcaster and former advisor to the Department of Government Efficiency (DOGE), Katie Miller also recently shared a post on X highlighting the impact of the project. In the post, she noted that the Musk Foundation donated ultraviolet water filtration systems and new drinking stations across all 12 Flint Community Schools buildings as well as the district's administration building. She also pointed out that the city separately provided free water filters for residential homes.Elon Musk's donations during the Flint crisisThe donation made by Elon Musk’s Foundation dates back to 2018, when the organisation contributed around $480,350 to fund water filtration systems for Flint schools and an additional $423,000 to purchase laptops for students. Around the same time, Musk also pledged that he would "fund fixing the water in any house in Flint that has water contamination above FDA levels," as the city continued to deal with the fallout from its water crisis.The water crisis at Flint started in 2014, when the officials switched to a cheaper water source, which led to widespread lead contamination of water that affected thousands of residents. The water crisis also led to national outrage and prompted support from charities, public agencies and private donors asking for help for the affected communities.Clean drinking water returns to schoolsAccording to a report by The Independent, students in Flint were eventually able to drink directly from school water fountains for the first time in years after the Musk-funded filtration systems became operational. The foundation donated 136 filtering stations that serve school buildings throughout the district. Speaking at a ceremony marking the rollout of the new fountains, Kevelin Jones, superintendent of Flint Community Schools, said access to clean water should be a basic necessity rather than something families have to struggle to obtain. Before the filtration systems were activated, the district had relied on bottled water for several years.The filtration systems use advanced technology designed to remove contaminants, including lead, from drinking water. Before being placed into service, they were tested by researchers from Kettering University and independent environmental experts to ensure they met safety standards.Delays before rolloutThe project also faced a lot of challenges. The installation of the filtration stations faced a lot of delays and also needed reconfiguration before they could be implemented completely. Once fully functional, the students welcomed the change after years without access to drinking fountains. One of the students also told the local media that it felt "amazing" to finally have clean water available at school. This change marked a significant moment for the district as it had depended on bottled water since the beginning of the crisis.Flint's recovery efforts continueThe residents however appreciated the support, but some community leaders also agreed that water filters alone cannot solve the bigger problems caused on the infrastructure due to this water crisis. Former Flint Mayor Karen Weaver said in 2018 that in order to completely restore the trust of the public we need to replace the damaged water infrastructure and also lead service lines throughout the city.Since then, Flint has continued its recovery efforts. City officials have reported significant progress in inspecting service lines and replacing thousands of lead and galvanized steel pipes as part of the long-term effort to restore confidence in the city's water system.You use AI every day. articles.title: Pakistan to send astronaut to China’s space station aboard Shenzhou-24 mission
articles.summary: A Pakistani astronaut will join the crew of China's Shenzhou-24 spacecraft this year, becoming the first foreign national to visit Beijing's space
articles.body: A Pakistani astronaut will join the crew of China's Shenzhou-24 spacecraft this year, becoming the first foreign national to visit Beijing's space station, Chinese state media reported on Saturday.The astronaut will undertake a short-term stay in orbit before returning to Earth aboard the Shenzhou-23 spacecraft, according to the China Manned Space Agency.The agency has not announced the launch date or identified the astronaut.The mission will mark the first joint spaceflight involving Chinese and foreign astronauts in the history of China's manned space programme, news agency Xinhua reported.The Pakistani astronaut will participate as a payload specialist, according to Chinese broadcaster CCTV.Two Pakistani candidates underwent training in ChinaEarlier this year, two Pakistani candidates, Muhammad Zeeshan Ali and Khurram Daud, had begun training alongside their Chinese counterparts. One of them was expected to be selected for the short-duration mission.The training included developing hands-on operational capabilities as well as intensive Chinese language instruction.The two candidates had been training at the China Astronaut Research and Training Centre in Beijing, according to a Pakistani space agency official.The mission is part of an agreement signed by China and Pakistan in February 2025. It also forms part of the two countries' broader cooperation in space exploration under Beijing's Belt and Road Initiative.China and Pakistan expand space cooperationPakistan has also outlined wider ambitions for its space programme. Planning minister Ahsan Iqbal said last month that the country aims to land on the Moon by 2035.Pakistan and China are also collaborating on a Pakistani-built lunar rover for China's Chang'e-8 mission, expected around 2028. The rover is intended to use artificial intelligence-based stereo imaging to identify obstacles, assess distances and navigate the lunar surface autonomously.The lunar rover project is separate from Pakistan's stated ambition to achieve a lunar landing by 2035.A Pakistani space agency official told Reuters last month that there was no official commitment or discussion about sending a Pakistani astronaut to the Moon under the existing partnership.China plans crewed Moon landing by 2030China is preparing for its first crewed lunar landing by 2030.The United States is seen as its main rival in space exploration, with Nasa aiming to land astronauts on the lunar surface in 2028.India, meanwhile, has set a target of sending an astronaut to the Moon by 2040 and establishing its own space station by 2035.Its Gaganyaan programme aims to conduct its first crewed orbital mission by 2027, following planned uncrewed missions.

articles.title: 14-year Himalayan study of 25,604 arthropods finds fewer spiders but more grasshoppers, ticks and mites when livestock replace native grazers
articles.summary: A 14-year experiment in the cold deserts of northern India’s Trans-Himalayan ecosystem has found that replacing native grazers with livestock changes the
articles.body: A 14-year experiment in the cold deserts of northern India’s Trans-Himalayan ecosystem has found that replacing native grazers with livestock changes the abundance of ground-dwelling arthropods. Researchers analysed 25,604 arthropods collected using pitfall traps over 2,765 trap-days during spring, summer and autumn.The study examined how different grazing regimes affected these small animals and found clear differences between areas grazed by livestock and those used by native herbivores. According to research published in Ecological Applications titled, ‘Replacing native grazers with livestock influences arthropods to have implications for ecosystem functions and disease’, spiders were less abundant under livestock grazing, while grasshoppers, ticks and mites were more abundant.A 14-year experiment examined the effects of livestock grazingThe researchers used a replicated, landscape-level grazer-exclusion experiment that ran for 14 years in the Trans-Himalayan cold deserts of northern India. They focused on ground-dwelling arthropods and compared responses to changes in grazing regimes, including situations where livestock replaced native grazers. The team assessed spatial and temporal variation in the abundance of the animals.Sampling took place across the growing season, covering spring, summer and autumn. Pitfall traps were used to collect the specimens, with the study recording 2,765 trap-days. In total, the researchers analysed 25,604 arthropods. The sampling approach allowed them to examine patterns across the landscape and through time, rather than relying on a single collection period.Grazer identity and environmental factors shaped arthropod communitiesThe 25,604 specimens belonged to 88 operational taxonomic units, covering six orders and 33 families. The groups included ants, wasps, bees, ticks and mites, spiders, grasshoppers and beetles. The researchers found that the composition of the grazer assemblage, whether livestock or native herbivores, had a strong influence on vegetation and arthropods.Their partial redundancy analysis showed that grazing and grazer identity, alongside variation in vegetation composition and soil variables, explained 53.6% of the spatial and temporal variation in arthropod communities.The analysis linked the differences in arthropod communities to grazing conditions and the environmental characteristics measured in the study. The findings showed that grazer identity mattered alongside grazing itself.Spiders, grasshoppers and ticks responded differently to grazer identityThe study found contrasting responses among different arthropod groups. Spiders, which are predators, were less abundant in areas grazed by livestock than in areas grazed by native herbivores. Grasshoppers, described as leaf eaters, were more abundant under livestock grazing. Ticks and mites, identified by the researchers as parasitic disease vectors, also showed higher abundance under livestock than under native grazers.The reduction in spiders could fundamentally alter the flow of material and energy through cascading effects caused by the loss of predators as per the researchers. They also noted that greater grasshopper abundance may contribute to vegetation degradation often associated with livestock. The results showed that different groups responded differently to the same grazing change.How does replacing native grazers with livestock affect ecosystem healthThe researchers said the increase in ticks and mites raised concerns about vector-borne disease and pointed to the need for planned interventions that align animal husbandry with One Health. They concluded that the loss of native grazers as livestock expand can have wide-ranging effects through changes in arthropods.These effects may influence ecosystem structure and functions, while also creating challenges and opportunities for reducing risks from vector-borne disease. The study examined the consequences of replacing native grazers with livestock in one Trans-Himalayan ecosystem, and its findings centred on ground-dwelling arthropods.

articles.title: Trump's makes nuclear push in space exploration, sets 2-yr deadline for Nasa's Mars mission
articles.summary: Mars could soon become the destination for a spacecraft powered by nuclear energy, as the United States prepares to take its deep-space ambitions beyond
articles.body: Mars could soon become the destination for a spacecraft powered by nuclear energy, as the United States prepares to take its deep-space ambitions beyond conventional rocket technology.President Donald Trump has announced that Nasa will launch its first-ever nuclear-powered spacecraft to the Red Planet within the next two years, marking a major step in America's push to develop advanced propulsion systems for future space exploration.Speaking at the UP Summit at Kennedy Space Center in Cape Canaveral, Florida, Trump said the mission would be part of his administration's broader ambitions to expand America's presence beyond Earth.According to a report by Fox News, he said, "Within the next two years, NASA will launch the first-ever nuclear-powered spacecraft to Mars."For Nasa, the planned Space Reactor-1 (SR-1) Freedom mission will mark an important step towards testing nuclear-electric propulsion beyond Earth's orbit. The spacecraft will use a nuclear reactor to generate electricity for its thrusters and is also expected to carry three Mars helicopters, building on the success of the agency's Ingenuity helicopter.Trump also linked the Mars mission to his administration's broader ambition of establishing a permanent American presence beyond Earth. He said the US would first return astronauts to the Moon and then work towards establishing a lasting presence on its surface.He also highlighted his recently issued 'American Declaration of Freedom in Space', which seeks to promote American exploration and settlement beyond Earth."Just this week, I issued the American Declaration of Freedom in Space, proclaiming all of space open for American settlement, American civilization, and American freedom," he said.Nuclear propulsion in space and why it mattersNuclear propulsion could transform how spacecraft travel through deep space by allowing them to cover greater distances, carry heavier scientific equipment and operate for longer periods.Unlike conventional chemical rockets, which burn fuel to generate thrust, nuclear-electric propulsion uses energy released through nuclear fission to generate electricity, which then powers electric thrusters. These thrusters accelerate electrically charged propellant to gradually push the spacecraft forward.According to Nasa, nuclear-electric propulsion produces relatively low thrust compared with conventional rockets but can operate continuously for extended periods while consuming significantly less propellant. This makes it particularly useful for long-duration missions where carrying large quantities of fuel is a major challenge.The technology could also overcome the limitations of solar power. As spacecraft travel farther from the Sun, sunlight becomes weaker, reducing the effectiveness of solar panels. A nuclear reactor, however, can generate electricity independently of sunlight, allowing spacecraft to operate in distant regions of the solar system.Nasa sees nuclear propulsion as a key technology for future deep-space exploration, including missions to Mars and destinations beyond it. In January 2026, Nasa official Greg Stover highlighted its potential, saying, "Nuclear propulsion has multiple benefits including speed and endurance that could enable complex deep space missions."
