articles.title: In 1935, a Black linguist recorded Louisiana Creole speakers on aluminium discs; researchers have now uncovered the earliest extended audio of a language that all but vanished from New Orleans by the 1950s
articles.summary: There is something extraordinary about how memory finds its way back to us through our senses.
articles.body: There is something extraordinary about how memory finds its way back to us through our senses. A familiar sound or voice can transport us to an entire world we thought existed only in the past. But if you were ever to hear the voice of someone who lived centuries before you, that sound could catapult you into a new world of memory and history, making it the most palpable realisation of a past only ever seen in photographs or recorded in texts.For a linguist, hearing the voices preserved in forgotten recordings has offered a profoundly original way of understanding how people spoke, the expressions they used, and how languages became distinct within their communities. With a collection of recordings made in Louisiana in 1935, the voices of people speaking a language that was once present in the social fabric and everyday life of New Orleans are now being brought back to life.How were the recordings captured and then researched?The recordings were made by Lorenzo Dow Turner, a pioneering Black linguist who travelled through Louisiana in July 1935 to document the speech and cultural traditions of Black communities. His work involved interviewing people from different walks of life, including plantation workers, teachers, schoolchildren and other residents. However, the recordings remained largely unexplored for decades, until Dr Oliver Mayeux, a researcher at the University of Cambridge, came across the collection while investigating Turner's work. The discovery has now provided linguists with the earliest known extended recordings of spoken Louisiana Creole and Louisiana French.Louisiana Creole, also known as Kouri-Vini, has a history closely connected to slavery and colonialism in the southern United States. The language reportedly emerged in the 18th century in communities along the lower Mississippi River, where enslaved West Africans and their descendants were brought into contact with French-speaking plantation owners and administrators. Many of the enslaved people came from different African linguistic backgrounds and did not share a common language. As elements of the French language came to be learned and adapted, a new language gradually developed, drawing vocabulary from French while establishing its own grammatical structure.Over time, Louisiana Creole became an important means of communication among working-class communities and people of colour across the region. It could be heard around New Orleans, including its port and neighbourhoods, as well as in the towns, farms and bayous of southern Louisiana. The language was not limited to any one social setting, and even some wealthier white families became familiar with it through the Black women who worked as their children's caregivers. However, the language gradually lost ground as English increasingly became dominant in public life and intergenerational transmission declined. By the 1950s, the New Orleans variety had largely disappeared from everyday use.The most notable opportunity that Turner's collection provides us with is the chance to hear the language instead of only reconstructing it from written material. Before the discovery, researchers and academics had largely relied on written texts and transcriptions to understand historical Louisiana Creole, or on scattered references in literary texts produced a century ago, predominantly by white people. So, for the very first time, when we get to hear the voices of the community itself, we are exposed to an archive of the Black community and its speech, where its members themselves are the narrators of their story.A look into the Creole language through the recordingsAccording to Dr Oliver Mayeux's published research paper, the collection consists of 13 aluminium discs, each measuring 12 inches and recorded at 78 revolutions per minute. Turner's recording equipment was far from the compact devices used by researchers today. It weighed more than 100 pounds and had a large microphone attached to it, making the process of recording people a rather unusual experience. He relied on a network of Black doctors and intellectuals who helped him find participants and provided access to their offices, which were trusted spaces during the period of racial segregation. The recordings were made in New Orleans, Lafayette, Chatagnier and Opelousas.Among the voices preserved on the discs is that of Emma Benoit, a sharecropper from the Lafayette area who was 69 when she was interviewed. She spoke about her life working in the fields, her marriage and the loss of her husband, who had died around two decades earlier. Her mother had been enslaved, making her account particularly valuable as a personal recollection of a generation whose experiences were rarely recorded in their own words. Another speaker, Odélia Edmond, born in New Orleans in 1862, recalled an amusing childhood incident involving a woman who sold brick dust. She remembered taking money given to her by her mother but never actually paying the woman, joking years later about the debt and whether she might have to repay it after death. Through repeated listening and comparisons with census information and archival material, Mayeux was also able to identify the people behind several of the recordings.Researchers and linguists have found that Louisiana Creole incorporated more French grammatical features than previously understood, with speakers sometimes moving between French and Creole during conversations. Some grammatical constructions, including the placement of articles after nouns, also differed considerably from contemporary French. The recordings therefore challenge earlier assumptions based largely on written accounts of the language. Although Louisiana Creole is now critically endangered, with only a few thousand speakers remaining, efforts to revive it have begun gaining momentum. Younger Louisianans are learning and teaching Kouri-Vini, creating online resources and encouraging new communities of speakers.Turner's aluminium discs were never intended to become a window into the lives of people nearly a century later. However, the survival of these recordings is serendipitous, giving us access to the life, language and ways of being that were sustained through words and voices. For Creole, a language so deeply shaped by displacement, slavery and generations of cultural exchange, these recordings open up a new pathway for examining the expressions of a community, creating gateways for further studies, understanding and an appreciation of the power that lies within language itself. It is a history that has existed in writing for generations, but is now waiting to be heard.

articles.title: A landfill near Istanbul generates electricity from captured waste gas, yet satellites detect methane escaping at about 7.4 tons an hour on average, new reporting finds as Turkey prepares to host COP31
articles.summary: The great mountain of domestic refuse outside Istanbul is doing more than just being the last stop for the rubbish of the Turkish city.
articles.body: The great mountain of domestic refuse outside Istanbul is doing more than just being the last stop for the rubbish of the Turkish city. This organic material breaks down under the surface, producing methane. This methane is captured and converted into electricity. Waste can be a resource for energy. But even with efforts to cut emissions, huge amounts of the potent greenhouse gas still leak into the atmosphere. As Turkey braces to host the COP31 climate summit, new satellite data have refocused attention on the country’s struggles to curb landfill emissions, reports Reuters.A major methane emitterResearchers at the University of California, Los Angeles (UCLA) analyzed satellite observations that revealed significant methane emissions from several Turkish landfill sites, Reuters said. The results were based on publicly available Carbon Mapper data from the Tanager-1 satellite from January 2025 through the end of May 2026.Analysis reported by Reuters found 70 methane plumes across Turkey’s 10 highest emitting waste sites. The emissions detected varied between 841 kg/hour and 7.4 metric tons/hour on average. Three of the big sites were found around Istanbul, while other sites were located near Ankara, Izmir and Antalya, and the city of Turkey is to host COP31 from Nov 9 to 20.The landfill near Seymen, west of Istanbul, had an average detected emission rate of about 7.4 tons an hour, putting it near the world's highest emitting landfill sites.Waste gas to power conversionThe Reuters report states that the Seymen facility receives about 8,500 tons of household waste daily, a significant portion of the estimated 20,000 tons of waste generated daily in Istanbul.The methane is produced as organic waste buried underground decays and is collected by municipal operator ISTAC, Reuters reports. The gas captured is then used by an energy company to generate electricity at a facility that began operating in 2020. The plant generates roughly 22,000 megawatt-hours of electricity every month, according to a 2025 report by the energy news website Enerji Gunlugu.Yet the existence of collection infrastructure has not stopped large emissions. Researchers have not yet figured out how much methane the facility captures, and ISTAC officials have questioned whether the satellite observations are representative of the facility's typical emissions.Representatives of the operator said emissions normally ran between four and six tons an hour. An unusually high satellite reading on one day was caused by maintenance work on methane collection pipes, an uncovered area of about 30 hectares and low atmospheric pressure, they said.Why cutting methane mattersMethane is the second biggest driver of climate change after carbon dioxide, with a warming potential more than 80 times greater than carbon dioxide over its first 20 years in the atmosphere. Cutting the amount released therefore has relatively rapid climate benefits.According to Reuters, Turkey is the world's fifth-largest emitter of methane from solid waste, behind China, the United States, Russia and Brazil, Climate TRACE says.According to data from the World Bank, Turkey’s methane emissions from the waste sector have increased nearly 25% between 2014 and 2024, compared to a 6.5% increase globally.COP31 attracts new scrutinyTurkey’s waste management system is an opportunity for large emissions reductions. “There is an opportunity to improve the gas collection infrastructure, to fix damaged landfill covers, and to divert organic waste away from disposal sites,” said Tia Scarpelli, waste sector lead at Carbon Mapper.Turkey’s Environment Ministry has been promoting its Zero Waste Initiative, which seeks to boost recycling and reduce the volume of waste going to landfill. The country’s waste recovery rate increased to 37.53% in 2025 from 13% in 2017, the report said.Turkey, however, is not a signatory to the Global Methane Pledge that was launched at COP26 in 2021 to cut methane emissions collectively by 30% from 2020 levels by 2030.Beyond climate change, the effectsCommunities near landfill operations also bear the burden. Residents of Seymen, a town about five kilometers from the waste site, say they have been bothered by bad smells, especially in the summer.Reuters said methane is odorless, but pungent compounds are emitted by decomposing organic waste. With COP31 on the horizon, Turkey has a major opportunity to demonstrate how better waste management can deliver tangible climate action. The challenge now is not just to produce electricity from waste material, but to do so without the additional cost of continuing greenhouse gas emissions.Image Courtesy: Reuters

articles.title: The UV-tracking Gem made me rethink how sunlight affects my health, not just my appearance
articles.summary: The90 Gem challenged my assumptions about sun exposure and got me thinking more about my health than skin aging, though its app guidance could be clearer.
articles.body: With temperatures rising to the 90s in Los Angeles, avoiding the heat wasn’t exactly an option while I was at a relative’s outdoor party in August. So I sat beneath a patio umbrella with a powerful fan nearby, figuring I was protected from the sun and heat. Half an hour later, I felt exhausted, dizzy, nauseous, and generally unwell, symptoms consistent with heat exhaustion. Around the same time, I received a notification from an app used by the $249 ($149 at the time of publication) UV-tracking necklace I’d been wearing, called Gem, from a company called The90. It warned that my UV exposure had climbed considerably. It turns out UV radiation wasn’t repelled by this patio umbrella, and it’s hard to ever be fully protected because radiation can be reflected or scattered by objects in the environment. While UV exposure and overheating are different things, I’d mistakenly assumed the shade and the fan would adequately protect me from both. This led to a discovery: One of my medications increases my sensitivity to heat, which helped to explain similar episodes I’d experienced over the years. The Gem didn’t diagnose anything, but it prompted me to investigate something I might otherwise have dismissed. Since then, I’ve been more mindful about limiting time outdoors during hours of peak heat and UV, staying hydrated, and paying closer attention to how I’m feeling outside. [Product: The90 Gem | I’ll admit my initial interest in tracking UV was largely vanity-driven. As much as I try to challenge harmful beauty standards, I’m hardly immune to them. Having started going gray in my 20s, I’m keen on slowing down other visible signs of aging where I reasonably can. But between being Indian (I rarely get sunburned thanks in part to my skin’s higher melanin content, not that it eliminates the risk of sun damage or skin cancer) and living within walking distance of the beach in perpetually sunny LA, I hadn’t given much thought to how much UV exposure I was actually getting. The Gem has helped me better understand it by providing a range of estimates, some more useful than others. The included UV-detecting sensor measures UVA and UVB radiation separately, rather than simply displaying my area’s UV forecast. UVB is primarily responsible for sunburn and helps your skin produce vitamin D, while UVA contributes to premature aging, even when you aren’t visibly burning. Thankfully, getting these metrics doesn’t come at the cost of wearing a bulky device. The circular pendant comes with a cute, thin necklace I’d happily wear even if it didn’t track anything. Its titanium, gold- or silver-colored chain pairs well with a variety of outfits. Battery life lasted almost exactly a week (the advertised lifespan), and the Gem recharges using an included charging dock. The90 plans to release a hat clip and bag tag early next year, which seem ideal for those who prefer not to wear it around their neck. [Image: The90 Gem’s modular design lets you detach the pendant from its necklace chain. The mobile app is central to the experience. It has easy-to-read graphs and jargon-light explanations. I enjoyed using it. While not required, you can create a skin profile so that it can estimate a range of metrics based on the sensor’s UVA and UVB readings. The profile is based upon factors like skin type, sensitivities, clothing, and sunscreen. That means its estimates aren’t based on UV exposure alone, though they’re still predictions rather than direct measurements of how your body is responding to sunlight. There’s a lot here, including your estimated vitamin D production, potential circadian light benefits, estimated nitric oxide-related benefits, cumulative UVA exposure, and recent accumulated UVA exposure. Alongside cumulative UVA exposure and weekly trends, its Skin Aging Zone assesses potential aging-related risk and offers personalized skincare advice. It also provides a personalized sunburn countdown, sunscreen reminders, and a daily Sun Score. The Sun Score is a rating that incorporates various metrics to balance sunlight’s potential benefits against the risks of overexposure. The company encourages users to aim for a daily Sun Score of 90, though more sun isn’t necessarily better. Too little exposure means missing potential benefits, while excessive UV can damage your skin. I appreciated the context, but the individual estimated measurements proved more revealing than the Sun Score. [Image: [Image: The UV readings in the app responded quickly as I moved between sunlight, shade, and indoors, even registering changes near windows. I couldn’t independently verify the sensor’s accuracy, but the readings behaved as expected as I shifted between environments. However, there were times when I noticed the Gem sometimes failed to register that I had been outside. Eventually, I discovered the app needs to remain running in the background (at least on iPhone; I haven’t tested on Android), as measurements aren’t stored on the sensor, and fully closing the app interrupts tracking. My experience at the outdoor party challenged my assumptions about how much protection I was getting from the shade. Just as surprising to me was learning how little UVB I accumulated during a typical week, despite living somewhere so sunny. I fell short of the app’s estimated sunlight-derived vitamin D target almost daily, prompting me to research how melanin, while offering some natural UV protection, impacts vitamin D production from sunlight. Until then, I’d mostly thought about sun exposure in terms of protecting my skin from damage. Seeing how little UVB I was accumulating made me consider what I might be missing out on, too. The vitamin D countdown wasn’t as helpful as I had hoped. During one test, its estimate of how much additional sunlight I needed dropped from several hours to under an hour, then climbed past six hours just minutes later. The fluctuations appeared related to changing UVB intensity, though I couldn’t verify that. I noticed similar fluctuations in the app’s estimated time to sunburn. With both countdowns changing so dramatically, I stopped paying much attention to the exact times and focused instead on the broader picture: whether it felt like I was getting too much or too little sun. [Image: I appreciated how the Gem encouraged me to think more about my health than simply preventing wrinkles. That was perhaps the biggest surprise of testing the Gem. After my experience using it at the outdoor party in August, I’d expected it just would encourage me to spend less time in the sun each day. In reality, my exposure often falls at one of two extremes: either too little to meet the app’s estimated targets or enough to raise concerns about overexposure, even when I thought I was protected by the shade. I now try to be more mindful about my UV exposure, even when I’m not using the Gem. I try to limit time spent outdoors during peak UV hours, and I try to get some sunlight on days spent mostly indoors. I credit the Gem with helping me better understand how my time outside could affect my well-being in ways I’d never considered, though the usefulness of your findings may vary. At $249 outside of a deal, it’s expensive, though it’s nice that it doesn’t have a subscription. I personally can’t justify the price given how much time I spend indoors, but I see the appeal for people who spend considerable time outside, or those who want to be more mindful of sun protection. For the price, I wish the app’s guidance was clearer at times, and I wish it could track UV without the app being open in the background, but the Gem ultimately got me thinking less about how my body looks and more about how I’m treating it. Photography by Sheena Vasani / The Verge

articles.title: Scientists discovered hundreds of sensory hair cells across the entire surface of squid bodies, not just their heads and arms; the finding may offer a new way to study how human hearing cells fail
articles.summary: The evolution of life on Earth is largely interconnected with living organisms sharing characteristic features among themselves.
articles.body: The evolution of life on Earth is largely interconnected with living organisms sharing characteristic features among themselves. These connections often help scientists to deduce indirect conclusions about various living beings by observing patterns across species. Recently, the discovery of previously unknown sensory hair cells on the body of squids has offered the scientists a new way to investigate how human hearing works. The findings, led by researchers at Case Western Reserve University, were published in the journal Current Biology in September 2026.The research titled ‘An anatomical map of squid lateral lines’ has found that sensory hair cells are spread all across the body of a squid and not just around their heads and arms. These microscopic structures help the animals sense movements in the surrounding water. The recent study includes the first full-body mapping of lateral lines on squid, which are made up of arrays of hair cells.Squids are remarkable marine creatures that change color, evade predators and move through the dark ocean. For a long time, scientists believed that squids have cells with many hair-like protrusions, similar to the ones present in the human ear that allow us to hear. These were believed to be present only on their heads and arms. Now, researchers have found out that such cells, called hair cells, occur on the entire surface of a squid’s body.The team of researchers used light sheet microscopy for this experiment. It is a state-of-the-art imaging process that uses a laser to create a thin sheet of light, illuminating just one plane of the specimen at a time. This allows researchers to build detailed 3D images and minimize damage to the tissue.How do squid “hear” without ears like ours?The human hearing mechanism depends on tiny sensory cells that are found deep inside our inner ear, in a snail-shaped structure called the cochlea. The sound waves create vibrations when they enter the ear, bending the hair-like projections on these cells. These cells then convert that movement into electrical signals that are transmitted to the brain, where they are interpreted as sound. Any damage to these delicate structures can lead to issues in hearing ability including hearing loss in extreme cases.Squid, like other sea creatures, use similar-looking sensory machinery for a different purpose. Rather than relying on ears like ours, they use hair cells on their bodies to detect local movements in the surrounding water. A passing animal, a shifting current or another disturbance can produce movements that these specialised cells register. The similarity in mechanism of detecting movements to understand different pitches of sound led the scientists to conclude that the skin of the squid seems to act like a human ear.The fascinating part is that unlike fish lateral lines which have hair bundles that do not vary in length, squid have hair bundles that appear to vary in length. According to the researchers, this variation may help the cells respond to different frequencies of water movement, much as the human ear. This distinction in squids from other sea creatures have made them potential models to study human hearing.Could a squid help us understand hearing loss?The hair cells inside our ears are extraordinarily delicate. When their sensory bundles are damaged, they may no longer transmit sound information properly. Such damage can occur through exposure to loud noise, ageing, certain medications or inherited conditions.Unlike some other cells in the body, damaged human inner-ear sensory hair cells generally do not regenerate naturally in a way that restores normal hearing. This is one reason researchers continue to investigate how these cells develop, function and become damaged.Studying them directly in humans presents challenges. The cochlea is small, intricate and protected deep inside the skull. Squid, by contrast, have hair cells distributed on the outside of their bodies, making their sensory structures more accessible for observation. That accessibility could give researchers an opportunity to investigate how hair bundles are built, how their lengths are controlled and how they respond to mechanical stimulation.

articles.title: Meet 15-year-old Rodion Zaichikov, the Luxembourg student who built an arc-jet wind tunnel to test a scramjet above 3,000°C and won the Ellison Scholars Prize at Europe's young-scientist contest
articles.summary: The story of the falling apple is perhaps the most famous account of how Isaac Newton's curiosity led to a scientific discovery that would go on to shape
articles.body: The story of the falling apple is perhaps the most famous account of how Isaac Newton's curiosity led to a scientific discovery that would go on to shape our understanding of the world and influence everyday life for centuries. From the telephone invented by Alexander Graham Bell to penicillin discovered by Alexander Fleming, science has always evolved because someone, somewhere got curious about a phenomenon they noticed. One such curiosity led 15-year-old Rodion Zaichikov to build an arc-jet wind tunnel to test a scramjet. In September 2026, Rodion Zaichikov, a student at the International School Luxembourg, won the Ellison Scholars Prize at the 37th European Union Contest for Young Scientists (EUCYS) in Kiel, Germany.His award-winning project is titled 'Expanding low-cost hypersonic wind tunnel with arc jet capabilities’. The project explores how to recreate extreme flight conditions to test a scramjet using intricate equipment that he constructed himself. His attempt at recreating this technology by himself also led to the questions around accessibility of such complex technologies. Rodion Zaichikov’s story is one that reflects what happens when a teenager decides to move beyond the usual school science projects to pursue ideas that seem impossible.The YouTube sparkZaichikov's interest took shape after he watched a video of an arc jet in operation. Rather than simply admiring the technology, he wondered whether he could build one himself.An arc jet uses electrical energy to heat a gas to extremely high temperatures, helping researchers simulate some of the extreme conditions encountered during high-speed flight. Zaichikov combined this technology with a specially shaped nozzle which allowed him to create a test device designed to test hypersonic airflow and a model of a scramjet engine.The idea is significant because equipment capable of reproducing such conditions is generally expensive and relatively rare. As the project's description on the University of Kiel's EUCYS website explains, the limited availability of arc-jet facilities can make it difficult for smaller research groups and start-ups to investigate hypersonic technology. Zaichikov's ambition was to explore a more affordable alternative.What exactly is a scramjet, anyway?A scramjet, short for supersonic combustion ramjet, is an air-breathing engine designed to operate at extremely high speeds. Unlike conventional jet engines, it relies on the vehicle's forward motion to compress incoming air, rather than using a compressor driven by rotating machinery. Crucially, the air continues moving at supersonic speeds through the engine's combustion chamber.Why does that matter? At hypersonic speeds, generally defined as Mach 5 and above, the air surrounding a vehicle behaves very differently from the air encountered during an ordinary flight. Shock waves, intense heating and complex airflow patterns make designing and testing aerospace vehicles a challenging task. Thus, the wind tunnels and arc jets allow researchers to investigate how engines and materials behave under conditions that would be difficult, dangerous or impractical to reproduce in ordinary flight tests.Zaichikov's device combines a specially designed convergent-divergent nozzle with an arc jet to investigate these extreme conditions. His apparatus enabled him to test a scramjet engine model at temperatures exceeding 3,000°C.The challenge wasn't just the heatFor Zaichikov, one of the biggest headaches was the vacuum chamber. The design flaw was that it kept leaking, forcing him to search for 3D-printable material capable of maintaining an airtight seal.He also built his own Schlieren imaging system, a technique used to make changes in air density visible. Because air is normally transparent, observing the shock waves and density variations associated with high-speed airflow is not as simple as pointing a camera at the experiment. Schlieren imaging makes these otherwise invisible changes observable.Together, the apparatus and imaging system allowed him to investigate airflow around his engine modelA prize, and years of curiosity behind itZaichikov's success did not materialise overnight. The Fondation Jeunes Scientifiques Luxembourg (FJSL), which supports young researchers, first encountered him when he was 11. Since then, he has participated in its programmes and represented Luxembourg at international science events.His list of experiences is quite extensive for a fifteen year old. Rodion visited the Eurospace Center in 2022 and attended the Mobisciences programme in Morocco in 2023. In 2024, he also received the best international project at the Mostra Nacional de Ciência which is a national science exhibition in Portugal. Then in 2025, he received an engineering award at the Taiwan International Science Fair. The recent EUCYS prize in 2026 marked just another milestone in his growing scientific journey that is only beginning.The European Union Contest for Young Scientists (EUCYS) brings together talented young researchers to present projects spanning different scientific and engineering disciplines. The 2026 edition took place in Kiel from September 22 to 27, with participants representing countries across Europe and beyond. The Ellison Scholars Prize recognises promising young scientific talent and is sponsored by the Ellison Institute of Technology, which works on technological solutions to major global challenges.For Zaichikov, however, the prize is not the end of the experiment. He has expressed an interest in continuing to develop his ideas, with a long-term ambition of creating a fully controllable vehicle capable of returning to Earth. That is a substantial goal, even for an experienced aerospace engineer. For a 15-year-old, it offers a glimpse of just how far his curiosity might take him.

articles.title: Want to fly to the moon? NASA is looking for new astronauts to help grow its Artemis program
articles.summary: NASA officials announced the news Saturday during a Kennedy Space Center air show promoting lunar exploration as well as advances in aviation and technology.
articles.body: CAPE CANAVERAL, Fla. — Want to fly to the moon and help build a permanent lunar base? NASA is accepting applications for a new astronaut class that will help grow the Artemis program. Officials announced the news Saturday during a Kennedy Space Center air show promoting lunar exploration as well as advances in aviation and technology. NASA’s last call for new astronauts was two years ago. More than 8,000 applied, with 10 making the final cut in September 2025. With only 32 active astronauts, the space agency needs more recruits as it looks to expand humanity’s presence beyond low-Earth orbit as quickly as possible. April’s lunar flyaround by the Artemis II crew kicked off the lunar campaign. “We have far more work than we have astronauts,” Artemis III commander Randy Bresnik told The Associated Press on Saturday. Aspiring astronauts have between now and Dec. 3 to submit their applications. NASA expects to make its final selection by late 2027, with the new candidates beginning their training by early 2028 — the same year that NASA intends to return astronauts to the lunar surface after an absence of more than half a century. By then “we’re going to have people on the moon — so don’t delay,” Bresnik urged potential candidates. Bresnik and his three crewmates will blast into orbit next summer to practice docking their capsule with a pair of lunar landers, one built by Elon Musk’s SpaceX and the other by Jeff Bezos’ Blue Origin. Their mission will stick close to Earth — no lunar flyby — and serve as a dress rehearsal for the following year’s Artemis IV mission that will attempt to land two astronauts near the lunar south pole. The moon base will materialize as more rovers, robots, structures and power grids are launched. Patience is essential for becoming an astronaut, noted Artemis III’s Frank Rubio, whose 371 consecutive days in space is a U.S. endurance record. Candidates must also be U.S. citizens with college degrees and professional work experience. The two years of mandatory training can be grueling, and it could take another several years on top of that before finally rocketing into space. “It’s important for them to realize most of that work is not going to the moon, right?” Rubio told the AP. “That will be about 1% of your experience. What you’re doing is contributing to the mission of going to the moon.” This will be NASA’s 25th astronaut class since the original Mercury Seven in 1959.

articles.title: A moth collected by Alfred Russel Wallace nearly 170 years ago was rediscovered in a museum drawer and helped identify 11 new species
articles.summary: A battered moth that had spent decades overlooked in the Natural History Museum's collection has helped scientists identify 11 species previously unknown
articles.body: A battered moth that had spent decades overlooked in the Natural History Museum's collection has helped scientists identify 11 species previously unknown to science. The tiny specimen was collected in Sarawak, Borneo, by British naturalist Alfred Russel Wallace around 1855-1856, but its significance went unnoticed for generations. Consisting of little more than a thorax and a pair of wings, it had even been dismissed by an earlier expert as unworthy of further attention. Modern DNA sequencing and research into its original labels eventually revealed its identity, allowing scientists to revive an entire moth genus.Alfred Russel Wallace's forgotten moth was found among millions of museum specimensThe discovery came while Natural History Museum scientific associate Mark Sterling and senior curator Dr David Lees were examining a collection of small, snow-white moths from Southeast Asia. They were investigating several specimens that appeared to represent previously undescribed species when an old, damaged moth became central to their research. The specimen had originally been described in 1863, but its deteriorated condition made identification difficult. In 1927, moth expert Edward Meyrick had recommended that it was 'better neglected'. Sterling and Lees took a closer look after noticing clues on its original labels, which suggested a much more significant history.A tiny label connected the moth to Wallace's expedition in BorneoOne of the specimen's labels carried the abbreviation 'SAR', which caught the researchers' attention. The letters stood for Sarawak, a region in what is now Malaysian Borneo that Wallace visited during his travels through Southeast Asia. The researchers compared the label with historical records and Wallace's own account of his expedition, published in The Malay Archipelago. His writings described collecting moths from a bungalow near Kuching, Sarawak, between December 1855 and January 1856. The location and other historical evidence helped Sterling and Lees establish that the damaged specimen had been collected by Wallace during that period, almost 170 years earlier.DNA sequencing helped scientists revive the forgotten moth genus TopirisThe researchers used a new DNA sequencing technique being trialled at the Museum to examine the specimen. Even though the moth was badly damaged, they were able to extract a tiny piece of its leg and obtain genetic information. The results showed that it belonged to the same species as more recently collected specimens from nearby Brunei. Further analysis established that the other moths under investigation also belonged to the genus Topiris. The findings allowed the researchers to resurrect the genus, which had effectively fallen out of scientific use following the earlier dismissal of the original specimen. The study was subsequently published in the journal ZooKeys.Eleven new moth species were named, including one after Greta ThunbergThe research expanded Topiris into a group of 14 species, 11 of which were newly described by scientists. Among the newly named moths were species inspired by the fictional characters Snow White and Cinderella, while another was named in honour of environmental activist Greta Thunberg. The discovery demonstrated how historical museum collections can still contribute to modern scientific research, even when individual specimens appear too damaged to be useful. The butterfly and moth collection contains approximately 13.5 million specimens, representing more than 100,000 species. The Wallace moth's rediscovery showed that overlooked material stored in museum drawers can still hold important clues about biodiversity and evolution.

articles.title: Scientists identify a completely new type of rock in a Martian meteorite and find garnet on Mars for the first time, but its planetary origin remains unconfirmed
articles.summary: An international team of scientists has identified a completely new type of rock on Mars and, for the first time, found the mineral garnet in a Martian
articles.body: An international team of scientists has identified a completely new type of rock on Mars and, for the first time, found the mineral garnet in a Martian sample. The discovery came from a fragment of the Martian meteorite NWA 8171, held in the Royal Ontario Museum’s collections, and was led by Tanya Kizovski of Brock University. According to the University of Portsmouth, the find offers a rare glimpse into the planet’s ancient past and could help researchers piece together its 4.5-billion-year geological history. Its Martian origin has not yet been confirmed.How did scientists identify garnet on Mars for the first timeThe team found garnet, a mineral that had not been identified on Mars until now. On Earth, garnet is a dark-red gem that was popular with the Ancient Egyptians, Romans and the Victorian elite, and it is the birthstone for January. The university also describes it as a cornerstone mineral in geology.Garnet provides a record of the tectonic forces, ore-forming processes and fluid-rock interactions that shape Earth's crust and mantle. In its account of the Martian find, the garnet is described as a new geological time capsule. It preserves clues about the temperatures, pressures and processes that shaped the planet billions of years ago.How did scientists discover garnet in the NWA 8171 Martian meteoriteThe research was led by Tanya Kizovski, Assistant Professor of Earth Sciences at Brock University. She and colleagues at the ROM learned of the garnet while analysing a fragment of a Martian meteorite known as NWA 8171, which is held in the ROM's collections. Kizovski set out to identify the fragment's minerals and chemical composition.The university reports that Kizovski found the section of meteorite interesting and the chemistry slightly unusual. The team first assumed the mineral was pyroxene, which is very common, but decided to look again. The analysis used the University of Portsmouth Electron Microscopy and Microanalysis Unit and the ROM's specialised laser equipment, and the team was surprised to find garnet. Professor James Darling of Portsmouth's School of the Environment and Life Sciences was part of the research team.What geological processes may have created garnet on MarsThe team analysed the fragment's chemistry and mineralogy and speculated about where the garnet came from. According to Kizovski, garnet is a classic example of a mineral often found in metamorphic rocks on Earth. Metamorphism transforms igneous or sedimentary rocks into a new form through exposure to extreme heat, high pressure or hot fluids.Kizovski said that on Mars, the heat and pressure needed to produce garnet through metamorphism could have come from a meteorite impact on the surface, from magma rising into the Martian crust, or from both. The university quotes her as saying the garnet-bearing rock type could give clues to how Mars has changed through its history. She also said it could give new insights into the ancient environments that may have formed the garnet and related minerals.How will scientists determine whether the garnet-bearing rock originated on MarsAccording to the University of Portsmouth, Kizovski cautions that the research does not definitively show whether the garnet-bearing rock formed on Mars. It may instead have been delivered to the planet and incorporated into its surface in a meteorite landing, which leaves open the possibility of an "extra-Martian" origin. Scientists now need to study the garnet's isotopic signatures to check whether it was produced on Mars or on another planetary body.Kizovski said measuring oxygen isotopes from the rock itself would help confirm a Martian origin or an exotic meteorite impactor. That process would destroy some of the sample, which has been avoided so far because of its rarity. Kizovski added that it may be the only garnet-bearing Martian rock available for study. ROM curator Kim Tait and Research Assistant Jessica Tomacic are continuing to study the sample together with Professor Darling. Kizovski said she hopes further work and more comparisons with rover and orbital data will reveal more about the origin and history of garnet on Mars.The project is funded in part by the Government of Canada's Natural Sciences and Engineering Research Council (NSERC) and the Killam Trusts Dorothy Killam fellowship. It also receives Science and Technology Facilities Council (STFC) funding at Portsmouth.
